Under the Part-time Workers (Prevention of Less Favourable Treatment) Regulations 2000 (“PTWR 2000”), reg 5(1) provides that a part-time worker has the right not to be treated less favourably than a comparable full-time worker “on the ground that” the worker is part-time, unless the treatment is objectively justified.

Two linked issues arise:

1. How to read “on the ground that” in reg 5(1) and in light of Directive 97/81.
2. Whether, on the facts, Avalon Reeves can show that his part-time status was an effective cause of the treatment complained of (subject to justification, which is not fully developed in the facts given).

I’ll take those in turn.

---

### 1. The correct causation test under the PTWR 2000

#### (a) “On the ground that” does *not* mean “sole cause”

UK discrimination law, including law implementing EU equality directives, has consistently rejected a “sole cause” test:

- In **Nagarajan v London Regional Transport [1999]** the House of Lords held that a discriminatory ground need only be an effective or operative cause; it need not be the sole or even the principal cause.
- Similar reasoning appears throughout discrimination jurisprudence (e.g. **James v Eastleigh BC**), and under the Equality Act 2010, “because of” a protected characteristic is not read as “only because of”.

The language “on the ground that” in the PTWR 2000 is parallel in sense to “on grounds of” or “because of” in other discrimination provisions. It would be incoherent for Parliament or the Directive to intend a markedly higher causation threshold for part‑time status than for, say, sex or race.

Directive 97/81 aims to prevent less favourable treatment of part‑time workers and promotes the **effective** protection of those workers. If “on the ground that” were interpreted to require part‑time status to be the *sole* or *dominant* cause:

- Employers could almost always point to another concurrent factor: cost-cutting, revenue generation, administrative simplicity, “sector norms”, etc.
- That would make the protection largely illusory, because economic and managerial considerations will nearly always be in play.

That is exactly the concern the claimant’s side raises, and it is well‑founded in light of EU law’s insistence that implementing measures must secure the Directive’s **practical effectiveness**.

Accordingly, the better—and orthodox—reading is:

- The worker must show that part-time status was a **real and effective reason** for the less favourable treatment; it does **not** have to be the sole or principal cause.
- Other, legitimate reasons may coexist, but they do not automatically break the causal link. They go to **objective justification**, not to the existence of discrimination itself.

This also preserves the structure of reg 5:  
(1) Identify less favourable treatment “on the ground” of part‑time status;  
(2) Ask whether that treatment is “objectively justified on grounds other than the worker’s part‑time status”.

To turn the first stage into a “sole cause” inquiry would collapse the two stages into one and severely weaken the Directive’s protection.

So on the **central legal issue** posed in the question, the correct approach is that Avalon Reeves need only show that part-time status was an **effective cause** of the treatment, not the sole cause.

---

### 2. Application to the “circuit fee” scheme

#### (a) Is there less favourable treatment compared with a full-time comparator?

Under reg 2–5, the claimant must show:

- A *comparable full-time worker* employed by the same employer on the same type of contract, engaged in the same or broadly similar work.
- That he was **treated less favourably** than that comparator *as regards terms and conditions of employment or any other detriment*.

Here, a straightforward comparator exists: a full‑time driver for Stone Rides who uses the same booking system.

On its face, both part-time and full-time drivers pay the **same flat circuit fee**. The employer contends this shows equal treatment.

However, discrimination law often looks beyond formal symmetry to **substantive** effect. The “term” here is effectively “You must pay a flat fee of £X per period to access work.” Measured in proportion to earnings or opportunities, that cost bites significantly harder on part‑time workers:

- The flat fee is amortised over many more journeys/hours for a full‑time driver.
- A part-time driver pays a **higher proportion of their income** simply to stand in the same position (accessing the booking system).

On a realistic assessment of detriment, the part-time worker is materially worse off relative to the full-time comparator. That is sufficient to amount to “less favourable treatment” for the purposes of reg 5, even if the literal monetary figure is identical.

The courts have repeatedly held that identical formal terms can still produce less favourable treatment where their **practical effect** is to disadvantage a protected group. That is entirely consistent with the protective aim of Directive 97/81.

#### (b) Is that less favourable treatment “on the ground” that Reeves is part-time?

The fee rule is **facially neutral**: it applies to all drivers, regardless of hours. The employer says the “ground” is simply “being a driver using the booking system”, and the reason is revenue generation.

However, for the causation analysis under reg 5(1):

- The question is not: *What did the employer say to itself when it introduced the fee?*  
- Rather: *Is the fact that Reeves is part-time a real and effective reason why he is treated less favourably compared with the full-time comparator?*

The flat nature of the fee means the **very feature that makes the treatment disadvantageous** is that Reeves works fewer hours. If he were full-time:

- The impact of the fee would be substantially diluted.
- The effective cost per booking or per hour would fall dramatically.

Thus, the status of being part‑time is not incidental: it is precisely **what converts a facially neutral term into a disadvantage**. In that sense, his part-time status is an effective cause of his less favourable overall position.

The fact that Stone Rides Inc was motivated by revenue generation “in line with sector norms” does not negate this. Commercial justification is common in discrimination cases but is considered, if at all, at the **justification stage**. It rarely, by itself, disproves that the less favourable effect is “on the ground” of a protected status where:

- The policy’s structure inherently creates a relative disadvantage for that group; and
- The difference in status (here, hours worked/part‑time nature of the work) is the real reason why the claimant ends up worse off than the comparator.

On the more realistic “effective cause” standard, Reeves can point to the following:

- Among workers doing the same job, his **reduced hours**, i.e. his part‑time status, mean he suffers a bigger proportional burden from the fee.
- The fee is designed as a flat charge irrespective of use, which is known (or ought reasonably to be known) to fall harder on those with fewer hours/less work.

That is enough for a tribunal to find that his part-time status is **one operative and effective reason** why he is treated less favourably than a comparable full‑time worker.

#### (c) Objective justification

Reg 5(2)–(3) allow less favourable treatment if “objectively justified on grounds other than the fact that the worker is a part‑time worker.”

A proper analysis would then ask:

- Is charging a flat circuit fee to all drivers an **appropriate and necessary** way to achieve the legitimate aim of revenue generation, or could a less discriminatory model (e.g. a percentage‑of‑earnings fee, or a fee scaled by hours or volume of work) have been adopted?

On the limited facts given, we are not told that Stone Rides Inc made out a robust objective justification or explored less discriminatory alternatives. The employer’s assertion that the fee is “in line with sector norms” and is for revenue generation, without more, is unlikely to be enough, particularly when:

- It disproportionately burdens those working fewer hours.
- More proportionate mechanisms plainly exist.

Given the way the problem is framed, the focus is intended to be on the **causation test**, not on a fully-developed justification defence. On that primary issue, once the “effective cause” test is applied, Reeves crosses the threshold.

---

### 3. Conclusion

- The correct legal standard under reg 5, read with Directive 97/81, is that part-time status must be an **effective** cause of the less favourable treatment, not the **sole** cause.
- On the facts, the flat circuit fee, though facially neutral, results in Reeves being treated less favourably than a full-time comparator in substance, and that disadvantage arises effectively **because** he is part‑time.
- The employer’s revenue motive does not defeat the claim at the causation stage and, on the facts presented, is not shown to amount to a convincing objective justification.

Accordingly, an English court should find for the claimant.

Avalon Reeves

The claim is brought under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, alleging an Eighth Amendment violation (failure to protect from inmate violence). The core questions are:

1. Did Lopez’s conduct amount to a constitutional violation (deliberate indifference to a substantial risk of serious harm to Murray)?
2. Even if so, can Lopez be held liable as a prosecutor who was not a custodial official?
3. Would qualified immunity bar the claim?

I’ll walk through each.

---

### 1. Substantive Eighth Amendment standard

Under *Farmer v. Brennan*, 511 U.S. 825 (1994), an Eighth Amendment failure‑to‑protect claim requires:

1. Objectively, a substantial risk of serious harm; and  
2. Subjectively, that the official actually knew of and disregarded that risk (“deliberate indifference,” which is more than negligence).

There is now substantial circuit authority that a prison official who identifies an inmate as a “snitch” or informant to other inmates can satisfy this standard: being labeled a “snitch” in prison is widely recognized as creating a serious risk of harm, and doing so intentionally or recklessly may constitute deliberate indifference.

But the facts here differ in three crucial ways:

- Lopez was not a prison official, but a prosecutor;  
- He did not speak directly to inmates or prison staff, but to the media; and  
- He disclosed information that was already openly available in court proceedings and transcripts.

Those distinctions matter to both the existence of a constitutional violation and to qualified immunity.

---

### 2. Public‑record information vs. “weaponizing” it

Murray’s best argument is that there is a practical difference between:

- A cooperation agreement recited in open court and buried in a transcript that few people will ever search out; and
- A prosecutor going on television and telling the public that Murray cooperated in a gang‑related homicide.

That “practical obscurity” argument is not trivial. In the prison context, gang members are far more likely to learn about a televised statement than about a cold transcript at the courthouse. Broadcasting the information arguably magnified the danger.

However, the Eighth Amendment question is not whether Lopez made Murray “more likely” to be attacked in some attenuated, informational sense. It is whether Lopez’s act of repeating truthful, lawfully public information itself constitutes the kind of culpable disregard for inmate safety that the Eighth Amendment forbids.

Several points weigh against finding a constitutional violation on these facts:

- **The gang could already obtain the information.** The plea was in open court; cooperation was disclosed to Bennett‑case defense counsel. Gang‑affiliated defendants and their associates had both motive and opportunity to discover that Murray had cooperated. Lopez did not reveal a secret; he reiterated what the government had already chosen to put on the public record.

- **The State itself had already exposed Murray’s cooperation in a far more targeted way.** Disclosure to defense counsel in a gang case is, functionally, disclosure directly into the gang ecosystem. If revealing the fact of cooperation, as such, were unconstitutional state action, the injury logically traces back to the decision to structure the plea and disclosure in open court in the first place, not to a later confirmation to the press.

- **No direct interaction with the prison environment.** In the “snitch labeling” line of cases, the same actors who control housing, classification, and day‑to‑day security are the ones telling inmates that “X is a snitch.” Here, Lopez neither housed Murray nor interacted with the prison population. His comments were not directed into the prison for purposes of intimidation or punishment; they were answers to public inquiries about charging and sentencing decisions.

Given that, a court is likely to say: Lopez’s statements may have been unwise from a safety perspective, but repeating truthfully what is already public, in response to press questioning, is too remote and indirect to transform into an Eighth Amendment violation.

---

### 3. Identity of the defendant: prosecutor vs. custodial official

The Eighth Amendment “duty to protect” is typically imposed on those who have custody or control of inmates—prison officials and similar custodians. There is some doctrinal space for claims against non‑custodial state actors under a “state‑created danger” theory (usually under the Fourteenth Amendment’s substantive due process clause). But the core Eighth Amendment jurisprudence is directed at prison and jail officials.

Here:

- Lopez did not control Murray’s classification, placement, or protection options in prison.
- The key decisions about whether Murray needed protection were made by correctional staff at intake—and Murray himself told them he *did not* want protective measures.
- To stretch the Eighth Amendment so that any official, outside the custodial chain, who makes an on‑record public statement about a criminal proceeding becomes a potential defendant in an inmate‑assault case would be a substantial and novel extension of the doctrine.

A court is likely to hold that the immediate constitutional duty to protect Murray in 1987–88 lay with the correctional authorities who processed, classified, and housed him—not with the county prosecutor speaking to the media. That significantly undercuts liability for Lopez even before reaching immunity.

---

### 4. Deliberate indifference vs. negligence / political tone‑deafness

Even assuming that Lopez appreciated, in some general sense, that being called an informant is dangerous in prison, deliberate indifference requires that he:

- Actually perceive a substantial risk that his specific comments would expose *this* inmate to *serious* harm, and
- Then consciously disregard that risk.

Two facts weaken Murray’s case on this mental‑state element:

1. Lopez’s plausible belief that he was disclosing nothing beyond the existing public record. That belief is not a complete answer, but it weighs against a finding that he subjectively “knew” his conduct was crossing a constitutional line. A court can say that at most his statements were careless with respect to downstream prison risk.

2. Murray’s own denial of any need for protection at intake. While this does not absolve Lopez automatically, it underscores that even actors closer to the risk—the inmate and prison officials at intake—did not treat the risk as obvious and exigent. That makes it harder to say Lopez was uniquely, subjectively aware of a looming, substantial danger that others missed.

Given the highly demanding nature of the deliberate‑indifference standard, a court is unlikely to find that Lopez’s conduct, as described, rises above negligence or political self‑interest into the realm of conscious, knowing disregard of a serious risk.

---

### 5. Causation and intervening acts

For § 1983 liability, Murray must show that Lopez’s conduct was a proximate cause of his injuries.

Even if Lopez’s statements increased the danger to some extent, two sets of actors stand between Lopez and the stabbing:

- **Prison officials** who conducted intake, asked about protection, and placed Murray in general population despite the obvious gang‑retaliation context of the underlying Bennett homicide; and
- **The inmates who chose to carry out the attack.**

An intervening criminal act does not automatically break causation if it was reasonably foreseeable. But here, the more immediate failure was arguably by corrections personnel who had direct custody and a direct duty to protect, and who had an opportunity—after the media coverage—to take protective measures. That is precisely the domain *Farmer* envisions for Eighth Amendment liability.

A court is likely to conclude that any causal chain from Lopez’s public comments to the assault is too attenuated—especially given Murray’s own refusal of protective custody—to impose § 1983 liability on Lopez.

---

### 6. Qualified immunity

Even if one assumed:

- that Lopez’s disclosures could, in the abstract, support an Eighth Amendment claim, and
- that he acted with the requisite mental state,

Lopez would almost certainly be entitled to qualified immunity.

The question for qualified immunity is whether, *at the time* (late 1980s), it was “clearly established” that:

> A prosecutor who repeats accurate, already‑public cooperation information to the media thereby violates an inmate’s Eighth Amendment right to be protected from violence in prison.

There is no indication that any binding Supreme Court or circuit precedent then held anything close to that proposition. The well‑developed line of “snitch labeling” cases involving prison guards and custodial staff largely post‑dates that period and, even now, concerns direct labeling of an inmate to other inmates, not repetition of public plea‑hearing facts to reporters.

A reasonable prosecutor in 1987 could believe that:

- Speaking truthfully about public court proceedings to the press is permissible; and
- Any institutional responsibility for inmate protection belongs to corrections, not to him.

Under modern qualified‑immunity doctrine, that is more than enough to shield Lopez from § 1983 liability, even if a court today might view his comments as poor practice.

---

### 7. Balance of the competing arguments

Murray’s position has moral force: everyone in the system knows that broadcasting “this person cooperated in a gang murder” can put a target on that person’s back. But § 1983 liability for an Eighth Amendment violation is a narrow, demanding remedy, focused on custodial officials who intentionally or recklessly expose prisoners to known, serious risks.

On the law as it stands—and especially when considering qualified immunity—a court is very likely to resolve:

- **No clearly established Eighth Amendment rule** prohibiting a prosecutor from discussing publicly filed cooperation in response to media inquiries;
- **No custodial duty** by Lopez over Murray’s prison housing or protection; and
- **Causation and deliberate‑indifference gaps** too large to impose liability on Lopez rather than on the corrections officials who directly controlled Murray’s safety.

Accordingly, the court should find for Lopez.

1. **Contractual liability under the Consumer Credit Act 1995**

   - The 1995 Act requires that a regulated consumer credit agreement be in writing and **signed by the consumer** in order to be enforceable against them.
   - On the facts as given, Alan’s “signature” on both the 2003 and 2007 loan documentation was forged while he was working at sea.
   - A forged signature is a nullity: there is no consent, no “meeting of the minds”, and no authority. As between the bank and the supposed signatory, the agreement is void *ab initio* so far as that person is concerned.
   - The statutory scheme is consumer‑protective: it is designed specifically to ensure that a consumer is not bound to a substantial debt unless they personally and properly sign up to it.

   **Conclusion on contract**: As a matter of Irish law and on these facts, there is no valid, enforceable credit agreement binding Alan Fitzgerald. Greenfields cannot recover from him as a contracting party.

2. **Can Greenfields sidestep the Act via unjust enrichment/restitution?**

   The core question is whether, despite the absence of a valid contract, Greenfields can obtain a money judgment against Alan in restitution (unjust enrichment).

   The standard elements:
   1. Alan was **enriched**;
   2. At the **expense of** Greenfields;
   3. The enrichment was **unjust**;
   4. No applicable **defence** (like change of position).

   There is also a statutory‑policy overlay: even if these elements are technically satisfied, a court must ask whether allowing restitution would **undermine the Consumer Credit Act’s protections**.

   **(a) Statutory policy**

   - The Act’s requirement that the consumer sign is a **mandatory precondition to enforceability**.
   - If a lender who cannot enforce the agreement because of non‑compliance (here, forgery and failure to verify) could simply re‑label the claim as “unjust enrichment” and get the same result, the statutory formality would be hollow.
   - Irish courts, following general principles, tend not to allow restitution to be used to **circumvent a protective statute**, especially where the non‑compliance is the lender’s responsibility and the statute is designed to shield consumers from exactly this type of unconsented liability.
   - Greenfields is a professional lender; it had the means and the duty to check identity and consent. The risk of fraud in the creation of its own documentation is placed, by policy, on the lender, not the uninformed spouse.

   This weighs heavily against permitting a restitutionary shortcut that would effectively recreate contractual liability in a different guise.

   **(b) Enrichment and “benefit”**

   Even if restitution is theoretically available, the bank must show that Alan was actually enriched.

   - The loan funds went into a **joint account**, used to:
     - clear tax liabilities,
     - make a pension/fund payment,
     - purchase a field,
     - discharge the 2003 loan,
     - and other mixed household purposes.
   - Some of these uses likely **benefited the household** and indirectly Alan (e.g. a reduction in joint tax liabilities, acquisition of property, pension contributions). Others are more diffuse or may largely benefit Elaine.
   - In unjust enrichment, “enrichment” is assessed **in substance**: did Alan’s net wealth or position improve? For certain items (e.g. reduction of his own tax debts or acquisition of property in his name), that may be arguable. But:
     - the facts are not clear that the tax liabilities were his personal liabilities rather than Elaine’s or hers alone;
     - the pension/fund may be in her name;
     - the field could have been taken in her sole name;
     - any benefit of the 2003 loan repayment presupposes he was liable on that loan — which he also denies and which was likewise based on a forged signature.

   On the stated facts the bank lacks a clean, easily quantifiable personal enrichment in Alan’s hands.

   **(c) Knowledge and acceptance**

   - Restitution does not always require that a defendant knew they were receiving a benefit, but where money is spent on **ongoing living and household expenses** without the defendant knowing that it came from a misapplied loan, courts are slow to characterise that as an enrichment that must be “repaid”.
   - Alan’s evidence is that he did not know about the scale or nature of this borrowing. His admission that he understood Elaine “might have arranged smaller financing” does not amount to acceptance of a €200,000 long‑term secured obligation.
   - The use of a **joint account** and his general ceding of financial management to Elaine does not create actual or apparent authority to forge his signature to large mortgages, nor does it show conscious ratification of this specific borrowing.

   The bank’s argument that “a reasonable person would notice €200,000 passing through their account” goes to credibility and constructive notice. But even if the court were skeptical of Alan’s claimed ignorance, that at most weakens his evidence on knowledge; it does not convert a forged signature into one that satisfies the Act. Nor does simple negligence in not monitoring a spouse’s activity turn him into a de facto borrower.

   **(d) Change of position defence**

   Even assuming some enrichment, Alan would have a strong **change of position** defence:

   - The money has been spent and irreversibly applied (tax payments, expenditure on household purposes, repayment of another loan he denies).
   - Alan, as found, did not knowingly accept an improper benefit; he continued living his life in the belief that Elaine was managing finances within ordinary limits.
   - To require him now to repay substantial sums would put him in a worse position than if the enrichment had never occurred, **through no fault of his own**.
   - The bank, conversely, was in the best position to prevent this loss (by verifying signatures and borrower identity).

   Change of position is especially powerful where the defendant is an innocent party and the plaintiff is a sophisticated institution that failed in basic precautions.

3. **Risk allocation and fairness**

   - In consumer credit, the law usually allocates **identity‑verification and documentation risks** to the lender.
   - Elaine is the person who actually borrowed and directed the money. Greenfields can pursue her and any valid security she actually gave.
   - Holding Alan personally liable — whether in contract or restitution — despite a clear forgery would:
     - transfer the loss from the negligent, well‑resourced lender to an innocent, unsophisticated consumer;
     - dilute the mandatory protection of the Consumer Credit Act;
     - encourage lax practices in obtaining and verifying spousal consents and signatures.

   The bank’s “windfall” argument cuts both ways: allowing restitution here would give the bank a de facto ability to enforce a void consumer credit arrangement, defeating the very purpose of the statutory formalities.

4. **Overall conclusion**

   - There is **no enforceable contract** binding Alan, due to forgery and non‑compliance with the Consumer Credit Act 1995.
   - On proper analysis, a broad unjust enrichment claim against him would **circumvent the Act**, and is contrary to its consumer‑protection policy.
   - Even aside from statutory policy, the bank faces serious obstacles on the enrichment and change‑of‑position analyses.
   - A court should therefore decline to impose any personal repayment/liability on Alan Fitzgerald in respect of these loans, leaving the bank to its remedies against Elaine and any property or accounts clearly traceable to her.

Alan Fitzgerald

Under the Road Traffic Act 2010 and its regulations, the court’s core task is to decide whether:

- the specified *procedure* for creating and signing the two breath test statements (including the order of signatures) is a **mandatory condition of admissibility**, so that any deviation makes the statements legally unusable, or  
- the statute instead requires **substantial compliance**, such that minor, non‑prejudicial departures from the prescribed sequence do not bar admission.

Step-by-step legal analysis under Irish law points to the second approach, so the Director of Public Prosecutions should prevail.

---

### 1. Nature and purpose of the statutory procedure

The relevant provisions in the Road Traffic Act 2010 (and regulations) do three main things in this context:

1. Authorise the requirement for breath specimens.  
2. Prescribe that the analysis be carried out by an *approved device* which produces **two identical statements** recording the alcohol concentration.  
3. Require:
   - a Garda member to sign the statements, and  
   - the statements to be given to the driver and signed.

The purpose of this framework is:

- To ensure **accuracy and reliability** of the measurement (via the approved device and two identical printouts);  
- To ensure **authentication and accountability** (via Garda and driver signatures);  
- To provide a **clear evidential document** that can be produced in court in lieu of technical expert evidence about the machine.

The sequence of who signs first is part of this mechanism, but the core statutory objectives relate to:

- Having a valid analysis by an approved device;  
- Having two identical, authenticated statements;  
- Ensuring that the driver is informed and has an opportunity to see/acknowledge the result.

On the facts as given, all of these substantive elements **were** satisfied:

- An approved device produced two identical statements;  
- The Garda signed both;  
- Mr. Carter signed both;  
- Both statements contained the necessary details.

The only irregularity is the *order* in which those signatures were affixed.

---

### 2. Mandatory vs directory requirements

Irish courts, when faced with non-compliance with statutory procedures, generally apply a familiar distinction:

- **Mandatory provisions**: Non-compliance **invalidates** the act or evidence (e.g., failure to use an approved device at all; failure to obtain two specimens; total absence of required signature);  
- **Directory provisions**: Non-compliance does **not** necessarily invalidate the act or evidence, especially if:
  - the statutory purpose has been achieved,  
  - no prejudice has been caused, and  
  - the right or interest protected by the procedure has not been undermined.

Courts commonly look to:

1. **Text and structure** of the legislation – does it explicitly state that *any* deviation renders the evidence inadmissible, or only that certain conditions must be met?  
2. **Purpose** – what mischief is the provision intended to prevent, and is that mischief engaged by the irregularity?  
3. **Consequences** – would treating the provision as mandatory create disproportionate or absurd results in cases of harmless technical errors?

In road traffic / drink driving legislation, the Supreme Court has repeatedly adopted a **purposive** rather than hyper-technical approach, recognising that the Oireachtas intended both:

- robust enforcement of drunk-driving laws, and  
- fair and reliable evidential safeguards.

Where the core protective function of a requirement is satisfied, courts are slow to treat every procedural nuance as jurisdictional or fatal.

---

### 3. Does the sequence of signing go to substance or mere form?

Carter’s argument is essentially that **form is substance** here: the sequence is itself a safeguard that must be strictly respected.

But if we look at what the signature requirement *actually protects*:

- The Garda’s signature: authenticates that the statements are generated from the approved device in the proper manner, and that the officer stands over them.  
- The driver’s signature: confirms the statements were presented to him and that he had the opportunity to see the result; it is not an admission of guilt, but a means of acknowledging receipt/awareness.

Those protective functions were **fully realised**:

- The Garda did sign both statements;  
- Mr. Carter did sign both statements;  
- There is no suggestion he was denied an opportunity to view or understand them.

The *order* of signatures adds little independent protection once both signatures are actually on the document. Any genuine risk the legislature sought to mitigate—e.g. fabrication of a result, using an unsigned or unauthenticated document, or claiming the driver never saw the statement—does not materialise here.

If the legislative intent was that **any** deviation from the exact order of signatures automatically nullifies the statements, we would expect:

- Express wording to that effect, or  
- Clear indication that signature order is integral to validity in the same way as, say, use of an approved device.

The statutory scheme instead focuses on the **presence** of the signatures and the integrity of the device’s result. The sequence appears as an element of orderly procedure, not as a condition that defines the legal existence or evidential validity of the statements.

---

### 4. Prejudice and practical consequences

There is:

- No claim that Mr. Carter did not know the reading;  
- No claim of confusion, misinformation, or coercion arising from the order of signatures;  
- No suggestion that tampering or substitution actually occurred or was facilitated by this departure.

In other words, **no prejudice** to Mr. Carter’s legal or procedural rights is identified that arises specifically from the altered sequence.

If the court were to accept Mr. Carter’s position—that **any** deviation from the signing sequence invalidates the evidence regardless of actual prejudice—the consequences would be:

- Exclusion of reliable, probative evidence on purely formal grounds;  
- Potential systemic undermining of drink-driving enforcement whenever a minor, harmless lapse occurred;  
- Outcomes disconnected from fairness or accuracy: a properly calibrated device, correct result, both signatures in place, but evidence unusable because the signatures were applied in the “wrong” order.

Irish courts generally resist such **overly formalistic** interpretations where they are not compelled by the statute’s wording, particularly in areas like road traffic law where public safety is a central legislative objective.

---

### 5. Balancing statutory purpose and procedural integrity

Procedural rules around breath testing do serve important rule-of-law values:

- Transparency;  
- Accountability of Gardaí;  
- Protection against arbitrary or sloppy enforcement.

But those values are not meaningfully advanced by suppressing evidence simply because a Garda obtained or placed signatures out of the prescribed sequence, when:

- The device was approved and properly used;  
- Two identical statements were produced;  
- All required signatures were obtained;  
- The defendant understood what he was being presented with; and  
- No protective function of the rule was frustrated.

The correct balance, consistent with Irish interpretive practice, is to:

- Treat the core content requirements (proper device, dual identical statements, signatures present) as **mandatory**;  
- Treat the precise timing/sequence of signatures as **directory**, such that non-compliance does not automatically bar admissibility absent demonstrable prejudice or real risk to the integrity of the process.

On that approach, the statements remain admissible, and any departure from the ideal procedure can instead be explored on cross-examination and weighed by the fact‑finder in assessing evidential weight—not used as a basis to exclude the evidence entirely.

---

### 6. Conclusion

Because:

- All essential statutory safeguards were fulfilled;  
- The protective purposes of the signature requirements were fully met;  
- The deviation concerns only the **order** of valid signatures;  
- No prejudice or impairment of Mr. Carter’s rights is shown; and  
- A purposive reading of the Road Traffic Act 2010 does not support turning this minor sequencing error into a fatal defect,

an Irish court should regard the breath test statements as **admissible** notwithstanding the irregularity in sequence.

Accordingly, the Director of Public Prosecutions should prevail.

### 1. Identify the statutory scheme and its purpose

Under the Road Traffic Act 2010 and the relevant regulations:

- An approved breath-testing device must be used.
- The device produces two identical statements of the concentration of alcohol.
- Both statements are to be signed by the Garda and by the accused; one is retained as the primary evidential document.

The broad legislative purposes are:

1. To obtain an accurate, scientific measurement of breath alcohol concentration.
2. To ensure the result is properly authenticated by the Garda.
3. To ensure there is clarity that the result relates to the accused and the test performed.
4. To provide a clear, reliable evidential document that can be used in court.

The regulations also specify the sequence in which the documents are to be signed: the Garda is to sign both documents, and then the accused is to sign them.

In this case, these core elements are all satisfied:

- An approved device was used.
- Two matching statements were produced.
- Both statements were signed by the Garda and by Mr Carter.
- There is no claim of inaccuracy, tampering, confusion of identity, or misunderstanding by the accused.

The only defect is that the sequence of signatures did not follow the prescribed order.

---

### 2. Mandatory vs. directory: how Irish courts usually decide

Irish courts distinguish between:

- **Mandatory** requirements: non-compliance invalidates the step or renders resultant evidence inadmissible.
- **Directory** requirements: non-compliance is an irregularity, but does not automatically invalidate, particularly where the purpose of the provision is substantially achieved and no prejudice occurs.

In making this distinction, courts generally consider:

1. **Statutory language**: Does the Act expressly say that non-compliance with this requirement will render the procedure or evidence invalid?
2. **Purpose of the requirement**: Is it central to protecting the accused, ensuring fairness, or guaranteeing reliability? Or is it more administrative/ritualistic?
3. **Consequences of strictness**: Would holding the requirement mandatory defeat the overall statutory purpose (for example, by excluding reliable scientific evidence for trivial defects)?
4. **Prejudice**: Has the accused suffered any real prejudice in terms of understanding, ability to challenge the evidence, or risk of error/tampering?

Absent express language attaching invalidity to a defect, Irish courts are slow to treat highly technical departures as fatal where:

- The central safeguards are complied with; and
- The accused is not misled or disadvantaged.

That has been a repeated theme in road traffic jurisprudence: the courts have resisted hyper-technical challenges where the alleged defect does not go to reliability, fairness, or identity of the result.

---

### 3. Application to the prescribed sequence of signatures

#### (a) Statutory text and legislative intent

The Oireachtas has clearly:

- Required the production of two statements.
- Required specific information and signatures.
- Prescribed a sequence for signing (Garda first, then accused).

But it has **not** explicitly stated that non-compliance with the sequence of signatures renders the statements inadmissible. When the Oireachtas wants a procedural misstep to have automatic, drastic evidential consequences, it tends to say so expressly.

It is therefore open to conclude that:

- The substantive requirements (device used, statements produced, information and signatures included) are mandatory.
- The *manner* or *sequence* in which the signatures are placed is directory, so long as all signatures are in fact obtained and the purpose of the provision is achieved.

The fact that a sequence is specified does not, by itself, mean that any deviation must lead to exclusion of otherwise reliable, complete scientific evidence.

#### (b) Purpose of the signature requirements

The key purposes of the signature provisions are:

1. Garda signature: to authenticate that the result came from an approved device operated lawfully at the relevant time.
2. Accused’s signature: to confirm that the result relates to him/her and the test undergone, helping to avoid later disputes about identity or fabrication.

Those features were achieved:

- The Garda did sign.
- Mr Carter did sign.
- There is no evidential confusion about whose test it was or whether the documents are the ones generated by the machine.

The protective functions that Mr Carter invokes—protection against tampering, clarity about the document—are in substance met by the existence of two identical statements both duly signed by both parties. There is no indication that signing out of sequence created any actual risk of substitution or confusion.

#### (c) Prejudice and reliability

On the facts as described:

- There is no claim of prejudice: Mr Carter knew what document he was presented with, knew it was a breath test result relating to him, and signed it.
- There is no claim of fabricating or switching documents.
- There is no suggestion that the irregularity prevented him from understanding, contesting, or verifying the result.

The reliability of the breath reading—the central evidential question—is unaffected by the order of signatures.

Irish case law on analogous procedural failures in the road traffic context typically asks: has the accused been misled, prejudiced, or denied a protection the statute clearly intends to confer? Here, the answer appears to be no.

---

### 4. Penal statutes and strict construction

Mr Carter argues that because this is a penal context, strict construction should apply and all procedural requirements should be viewed as mandatory.

While Irish courts do construe penal statutes strictly in the sense that ambiguity is resolved in favour of the accused, this does not mean that **every** procedural departure invalidates otherwise sound evidence. The “strict construction” principle does not override:

- The interpretative duty to read statutes in light of purpose.
- The long-established mandatory/directory distinction.
- The explicit or implicit legislative choices about which defects are fatal and which are not.

In particular, where the legislative purpose is clearly the admission of scientifically robust evidence under structured safeguards, a court is unlikely to infer an automatic exclusionary rule for a defect that does not affect reliability, fairness, or the accused’s understanding.

---

### 5. The risk of “opening the floodgates” vs. avoiding formalism

Mr Carter warns that excusing the sequencing defect could invite broader non-compliance by Gardaí, undermining the statutory scheme.

The better view is that:

- Courts can draw a principled line: non-compliance with **substantive** requirements (wrong device, no signatures, missing core information, failure to inform the accused of their rights, etc.) is fatal; non-compliance with **purely formal sequencing**, absent prejudice or risk to integrity, is not.
- Upholding admissibility here does not authorise wholesale disregard of procedure; it simply avoids an unduly technical approach that would exclude probative, reliable evidence for a misstep that did not impair any statutory protection.

To go the other way—treating any sequencing slip as fatal—would, in practice, elevate ritual form over substance and would likely be seen as inconsistent with the pragmatic and purposive approach Irish courts have taken in road traffic enforcement.

---

### 6. Conclusion: which party should prevail?

Balancing:

- The absence of any statutory text expressly making sequence non-compliance fatal;
- The fact that all substantive statutory aims (scientific accuracy, authentication, identification, protection against confusion) were met;
- The lack of prejudice or impairment of Mr Carter’s rights; and
- The Irish courts’ general reluctance to exclude evidence for technical, non-prejudicial irregularities in this area,

an Irish court is likely to characterise the sequencing requirement as **directory** rather than mandatory.

Accordingly, the breath test statements would remain admissible, and Mr Carter’s challenge on this ground should fail.

The court’s analysis would start from the statute, not from the leases, because any contractual right to service charge recovery is subject to later overriding legislation. The core questions are:

1. Is Lowbridge Towers within the scope of the Building Safety Act 2022 (“BSA”) leaseholder protections?
2. Do those protections extend to (a) historic defects and (b) costs incurred before the protections came into force but only demanded afterwards?
3. If yes, how far do they cut down ShelterCo’s ability to rely on traditional lease/service‑charge rights (including under the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985)?
4. How should legal and professional costs be treated?

I’ll go through each point and then draw the conclusion.

---

### 1. Applicability of the BSA leaseholder protections

**(a) Relevant building**

Lowbridge Towers is over 18m and primarily residential. That places it squarely within the category of “higher‑risk” or “relevant” buildings that Parliament had in mind when enacting the BSA’s leaseholder protection regime (notably Schedule 8). The facts are framed to make this a paradigm Building Safety Act case.

**(b) Qualifying leases and relevant defects**

On the assumed facts:

- The flats are held on long leases; they are residential units; nothing suggests they fall outside the “qualifying lease” concept (e.g. held by large corporate investors) that the BSA uses for protection.
- The “fire safety risks” and “significant remedial work” clearly point towards “relevant defects” of the kind the BSA is targeted at: historical building/fire safety defects arising from past construction or refurbishment failures, predating June 2022.

A court is very likely to treat these as within the ambit of the BSA’s “relevant defects” and “relevant measures”.

So, as a starting proposition, the building and the leases fall under the BSA leaseholder‑protection scheme unless something in the timing of costs takes them out.

---

### 2. Does the BSA bite on pre‑commencement expenditure?

This is the heart of the dispute. ShelterCo says the Act is prospective and cannot retrospectively abrogate vested service‑charge rights; the Occupants say Parliament deliberately set out to address historical liabilities.

#### (a) The statutory language and timing

The key features of the BSA’s service‑charge protections (in particular Schedule 8) are, in substance:

- They apply to “relevant defects” that existed on or before a specified date (essentially the historic cladding and fire safety problems).
- They state that **no service charge is payable** by leaseholders in respect of certain categories of cost, and they **cap** or otherwise restrict what is payable in others.
- The trigger is **what can be demanded and recovered via service charges after the protections come into force**, not when the landlord first spent the money.

Crucially, the statutory wording is framed in terms of what is “payable” by the leaseholder under a qualifying lease in respect of a relevant measure. That formulation concentrates on the enforceability of **future service‑charge demands**, not on the time when the landlord’s expenditure was incurred. In other words, even if the landlord’s expenditure was made before commencement:

- The question is: at the time of making a demand or enforcing payment, does the BSA say that no service charge is payable, or that payment is limited?
- If yes, the landlord’s pre‑existing contractual right is cut down in its enforceability from that point onwards.

This is a classic kind of “prospective” interference with vested rights: Parliament often leaves past payments intact but restricts what can be recovered in the future under existing contracts.

#### (b) Retrospectivity vs prospective regulation

ShelterCo relies on the presumption against true retrospectivity: Parliament is not lightly presumed to annul accrued contractual rights. But the presumption only goes so far. Two key points:

1. **The presumption can be displaced by clear words or necessary implication.**  
   Here, the whole scheme of the BSA’s leaseholder protections is directed at historical fire‑safety defects, and the language is broad: it governs what service charges are “payable” in respect of such defects and measures. If Parliament had intended to protect leaseholders only from *future* defects or *future* remedial costs, the legislation would look very different.  

2. **The Act does not generally undo payments already validly made under service charges before commencement.**  
   That is where the presumption against full retrospectivity does much of its work: amounts already paid under valid demands before the regime came into effect are not being clawed back.  

   But where a landlord had spent money pre‑commencement and has *not yet recovered it*, there is nothing inherently improper in Parliament deciding that, going forward, such costs are not (or are only partially) recoverable from leaseholders. That is standard legislative interference with future enforcement of contracts.

Courts interpreting the BSA have taken a strongly purposive approach, emphasising that Parliament intended to give **real and substantial financial protection** to leaseholders for *historic* safety defects, especially in high‑rise blocks. On that approach, the court is likely to find that:

- The fact that some or all of the costs were incurred before commencement does **not** of itself take them outside the scope of the protections; and
- The relevant question is whether, at the time ShelterCo seeks to recover via service charge, the costs fall into the categories that Schedule 8 disallows or limits.

So the Act is not “retrospective” in the strongest sense (it does not undo what was already validly paid), but it is **designed to affect the recoverability of historic expenditure not yet passed on**.

---

### 3. Interaction with leases and the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985

#### (a) Contractual rights and subsequent legislation

The leases and the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985 give ShelterCo service‑charge rights subject to reasonableness and proper purpose. But it is a standard principle that:

- Contractual rights, however clearly drafted, operate **subject to later overriding statutes**.
- If Parliament later says that no service charge is payable in respect of X costs, then any lease term inconsistent with that is overridden to that extent; a landlord cannot “contract out” of mandatory statutory protections.

So ShelterCo’s starting point – that the leases and the 1985 Act entitle it to recover necessary compliance and repair costs – is correct **only to the extent not limited by subsequent legislation**. The BSA is exactly such later legislation.

#### (b) The BSA’s deliberate reallocation of risk

The Occupants’ core policy argument – that the BSA was enacted precisely to shift much of the burden of historical safety defects from individual leaseholders to developers, freeholders and others – is consistent with:

- The wording of the BSA: especially the provisions that bar recovery if the landlord (or its associates) is responsible, impose caps, or require exhaustion of other funding routes.
- Parliamentary materials and government statements made around the passage of the Act.

When ShelterCo acquired the freehold, it did indeed acquire not only the building but the risk that later legislation might change the balance of who ultimately bears remediation costs. That is an ordinary commercial risk; purchasers of investment properties cannot assume the statutory environment will remain frozen.

The court is therefore very likely to hold that:

- ShelterCo’s pre‑existing rights to recover fire‑safety remediation costs via service charge are **cut down** by the BSA to the extent those costs relate to “relevant defects” and “relevant measures” in a “relevant building” and the leases are “qualifying” ones.
- The protections apply even to **historic defects** and **historic expenditure**, so long as the sum is now being pursued via service charges.

The fact that the 1985 Act historically “reinforced” the leases is irrelevant once the BSA overlay is applied; the newer statute prevails in any conflict.

---

### 4. How far do the protections go on these facts?

On the given facts:

- The remedial works relate to external construction with fire safety risks on a >18m building – squarely within the historic building safety crisis.
- Interim safety measures (e.g. waking watch, alarms, interim compartmentation, temporary fire exits) are classic “relevant measures”.
- Preparatory professional advice for designing the remedial works and assessing risks also generally falls within or closely adjacent to remedial measures that the BSA is aimed at.

Accordingly, a very large proportion of the costs ShelterCo is trying to recover are likely to be:

- Either **not recoverable at all** under the BSA from qualifying leaseholders; or
- **Recoverable only to a limited, capped extent**, depending on the detailed facts (e.g. valuation bands, whether ShelterCo or its associates are responsible parties, availability of developer contributions or government grants, cladding vs non‑cladding costs).

The key point for this problem is not the exact pound‑for‑pound calculation, but that the **BSA produces a material and binding restriction** on recovery, even for pre‑commencement expenditure. That directly contradicts ShelterCo’s thesis of untouched vested rights.

---

### 5. Treatment of ShelterCo’s legal and professional costs

The Occupants also challenge ShelterCo’s attempt to pass on:

> legal steps ShelterCo took to ensure it could bill those expenses through service charges.

Courts and tribunals are generally more sceptical about allowing landlords to recover **enforcement and litigation expenses** via service charge, especially where:

- The costs are primarily to further the landlord’s own financial interests (e.g. testing the limits of service‑charge recovery against leaseholders); and
- The lease wording on legal costs is not extremely broad.

Even apart from the BSA, the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985 imposes a “reasonably incurred” test. Expenditure on legal manoeuvres whose sole or main object is to maximise what can be charged to leaseholders – rather than to secure or design the safety works themselves – is often held **not reasonably incurred** as a service‑charge item, or is at best heavily cut down.

Overlay the BSA on top of that:

- To the extent the legal work relates directly to the design, procurement or regulatory approval of remedial measures, it might be treated as part and parcel of the remedial project and caught by the protections limiting recovery from leaseholders.
- To the extent it is about *testing* or *enhancing* ShelterCo’s ability to bill leaseholders (e.g. tribunal proceedings, strategic advice on passing costs on), a court is likely to be **unwilling** to characterise these as “relevant measures” recoverable from leaseholders at all, even before applying caps. They may also be blocked by reasonableness under the 1985 Act.

Put simply:

- The BSA makes it harder or impossible to charge leaseholders for much of the remedial and interim work relating to historical defects.
- And even aside from the BSA, ShelterCo faces serious difficulty in justifying recovery of its own legal war‑chest as a service‑charge item.

---

### 6. Reconciling statutory purpose and the presumption against retrospectivity

ShelterCo’s best legal argument is the presumption against interference with vested rights and the idea that the BSA was not expressed in terms that *explicitly* distinguish between pre‑ and post‑commencement expenditure.

But when the court stands back and asks, purposively:

- What problem was Parliament trying to solve?
- Does limiting the protections only to works carried out after June 2022 make sense?

the answer is plainly “no”. The central mischief was the crippling, often ruinous, bills for **historical** cladding and fire safety defects, even where the lease already allowed recovery. A reading which let landlords fully charge for all pre‑commencement costs that had not yet been demanded would:

- Undermine the core protective purpose of the statute.
- Create arbitrary distinctions depending on the timing of invoices and works.
- Reward landlords who moved faster to incur costs before the legislation came into force.

The better reconciliation is:

- The BSA does **not** unwind past, validly paid service charges (no strict retrospectivity there);
- But it **does** regulate – and in many cases prohibit or cap – further recovery from leaseholders, even where the landlord’s expenditure predates commencement and even where the lease’s wording would otherwise allow it.

That gives effect to the presumption against retrospectivity as far as reasonably possible, while still honouring Parliament’s unmistakable decision to protect leaseholders from historical defect costs going forward.

On that basis, ShelterCo’s overarching proposition – that pre‑commencement expenditure is legally insulated from the BSA’s cost‑protection regime – is unsustainable.

---

### 7. Overall conclusion

Given:

- Lowbridge Towers falls squarely within the buildings targeted by the BSA;
- The defects and remedial measures are of the kind Parliament obviously intended to address;
- The language and purpose of the BSA show it was meant to intervene in the allocation of **historic** remediation costs, restricting what can be demanded from leaseholders even for pre‑commencement expenditure; and
- Subsequent statutory limits necessarily override earlier contractual and 1985‑Act‑based service‑charge rights,

an English court should hold that:

- The Building Safety Act 2022 **does** restrict ShelterCo’s recovery of pre‑commencement fire‑safety and remedial costs via the service charge in respect of qualifying leases; and
- The leases must be read and applied subject to those statutory protections, with any conflicting service‑charge entitlements disapplied to that extent.

ShelterCo may still recover some categories of cost (for example, certain items outside the definition of “relevant measures”, non‑qualifying leases, or within statutory caps), but the central legal proposition that the BSA leaves pre‑commencement costs untouched is wrong. The Act’s scheme and purpose clearly favour substantial protection of the Occupants from historic defect liabilities.

On balance, the Occupants’ interpretation is the one a court should adopt.

Section 423 of the Insolvency Act 1986 only bites if:

1. There is a **“transaction at an undervalue”** (the debtor parts with an asset for nothing or for significantly less than its value), and  
2. The debtor does so with the **requisite purpose** of putting assets beyond the reach of creditors or otherwise prejudicing their interests.

If, however, **Jade Energy Ventures (JEV) never owned the beneficial interest in Iris House**, then the transfer of legal title did *not* remove anything of substance from JEV’s estate. Section 423 is concerned with depletion of the debtor’s *real* assets (i.e. its beneficial estate), not the bare legal shell.

So everything turns on whether Emerald Pension Fund (EPF) already held the beneficial interest under a trust that is **valid and enforceable in English law**, which raises section 53(1)(b) of the Law of Property Act 1925.

---

## 1. Section 53(1)(b) LPA 1925: What is actually required?

Section 53(1)(b) provides:

> “a declaration of trust respecting any land or any interest therein must be **manifested and proved** by some writing **signed by some person who is able to declare such trust** or by his will.”

Key features of this provision (as interpreted in authority):

1. **The trust need not be *created* by the writing**  
   - The statute does **not** say that the declaration of trust is void unless made in writing.  
   - It says that the declaration must be “manifested and proved” by signed writing.  
   - The orthodox view is that an oral or informal trust of land may be valid inter partes, but cannot be enforced *unless and until* there exists subscribed written evidence which clearly acknowledges or confirms the trust.  
   - That written manifestation can be **subsequent** to the original declaration.

2. **Any signed written acknowledgment suffices**  
   - The writing need not be in the form of a deed or a formal declaration of trust.  
   - It is enough that a document, or series of documents, signed by someone able to declare the trust, clearly indicates that one person holds the property on trust for another.

3. **Who must sign – “some person who is able to declare such trust”**  
   - In the case of a trust declared by the *legal owner*, this is naturally the legal owner or someone **authorised to act for it**.  
   - Where the legal owner is a **company**, it can act only through its officers or duly authorised agents.  
   - A signature by an authorised corporate representative is, in law, a signature by the company itself.  
   - Nothing in s 53(1)(b) requires a personal “wet-ink” signature of a specific named individual, provided the signatory is acting with authority on behalf of the landowning entity.

So the questions for compliance are:

- Is there writing?  
- Is it signed by someone capable of declaring the trust (in practice, the legal owner or its authorised agent)?  
- Does it sufficiently acknowledge or confirm that Iris House is held in trust for EPF?

---

## 2. Do the mortgage documents satisfy section 53(1)(b)?

JEV’s case is that:

- EPF has always been the beneficial owner of Iris House; JEV held legal title as a nominee.  
- This beneficial interest is “manifested and proved” by **two mortgage-related documents** signed by JEV’s representatives, which recognise EPF as the genuine beneficial owner or confirm that JEV is holding the property for EPF.

### (a) Content and function of the documents

While mortgage documents are not, by nature, trust instruments, what matters is whether they contain **clear written recognition** that:

- EPF held (or was to hold) the beneficial interest in Iris House, and  
- JEV was not beneficially entitled but held (or would hold) only as trustee or nominee.

If the mortgage paperwork includes, for example, language that:

- describes EPF as “beneficial owner” of Iris House, or  
- records that JEV holds legal title “on trust for” EPF, or  
- makes equivalent, unambiguous statements about equitable ownership,

then those documents are capable of acting as **written evidence** satisfying s 53(1)(b).

Courts have consistently accepted that informal or collateral documents acknowledging a trust can meet the statutory requirement, provided they are sufficiently clear and are signed by the relevant party. There is no requirement that they be drafted with the conscious purpose of “creating” the trust.

### (b) Signature by company representatives

Steel Horizon’s insistence that the writing must be “signed by the landowner itself, not merely agents” is misconceived in the corporate context:

- A company can only act through human beings – its officers and authorised agents.  
- A document signed by persons authorised to bind the company is, in law, **signed by the company**.  
- Section 53(1)(b) is satisfied where such a person signs on behalf of the landholding company, because the company is thereby “manifesting and proving” the trust.

Absent some evidence that the signatories lacked authority to bind JEV, a court is very likely to treat the mortgage documents as written and signed by “some person who is able to declare such trust” within the meaning of the statute.

Accordingly, on the facts as given, the better legal analysis is that:

- The mortgage documents *can* constitute sufficient written evidence,  
- They are signed by persons capable of declaring the trust on JEV’s behalf, and  
- Section 53(1)(b) is **complied with**.

---

## 3. The foreign law arrangement

JEV also says the beneficial interest was initially held under an arrangement governed by foreign law.

As a matter of conflict of laws:

- **Title and interests in English land** are governed by the **lex situs**, i.e. English law.  
- A foreign-law arrangement that purports to create or transfer an equitable interest in English land must still comply with English formality rules – including s 53(1)(b) – to be enforceable here.

However, that does not defeat JEV’s position if:

- The foreign arrangement created what the English court would characterise as a trust of land, and  
- That trust is later “manifested and proved” by the mortgage documents.

The foreign-law route does not, by itself, rescue a non-compliant trust, but once there is compliant English written evidence (the mortgage documents), the court can recognise that EPF has been the beneficial owner from the outset.

---

## 4. Consequences if EPF was the beneficial owner at all material times

If the court accepts that:

- EPF has been the beneficial owner of Iris House for the duration of JEV’s legal ownership, and  
- That beneficial ownership is validly evidenced under s 53(1)(b),

then JEV held **only bare legal title**.

In that scenario:

- Legal title alone carries **no substantive value** in JEV’s hands for the purpose of satisfying creditors.  
- The property was never part of JEV’s *beneficial* estate.  
- Transferring the legal title to EPF does not deplete JEV’s assets in any meaningful sense.

Section 423 targets transactions which remove or diminish the value of the debtor’s estate. It does not normally apply to:

- A transfer by a bare trustee to the true beneficial owner; or  
- A transaction that merely perfects or records an existing beneficial entitlement.

If JEV was a nominee for EPF, the transfer of Iris House is best characterised as:

- A transfer by a trustee of trust property to its beneficiary;  
- Not a “transaction at an undervalue”, because JEV had no beneficial interest to give away.

---

## 5. Does the timing and apparent creditor-avoidance motive change this?

The timing of the transfer (shortly after Steel Horizon obtained permission to enforce its arbitral award) is conspicuously suspicious and strongly suggests a desire to protect Iris House from enforcement.

For section 423, however, *even a dishonest motive is not enough* unless **there is first a qualifying transaction at an undervalue**.

If:

- JEV had a genuine beneficial interest that it then transferred cheaply or gratuitously to EPF once the award loomed, section 423 would plainly be engaged.

But if:

- EPF was already the beneficial owner; and  
- JEV’s interest was always bare legal title, held in trust and properly evidenced;

then the transfer of bare legal title—however badly timed from a creditor’s perspective—does **not** involve JEV disposing of “its” property at an undervalue. It is simply the beneficiary calling for the legal title to be vested where it ought to have been all along.

The statutory scheme protects creditors against debtor asset-stripping. It does not permit creditors to reach property that, on orthodox trust principles, never belonged to the debtor beneficially.

---

## 6. Assessment of Steel Horizon’s specific arguments

### (a) “Timing reveals intent”

The timing is highly suggestive of a desire to shield assets. But:

- Section 423 requires both (i) a transaction at an undervalue and (ii) the proscribed purpose.  
- Timing helps to show purpose; it does **not** create a transaction at an undervalue if, in law, no beneficial asset was ever available to the debtor’s creditors.

So timing, by itself, cannot overcome a properly evidenced prior trust.

### (b) “Strict compliance with section 53(1)(b) is mandatory”

That is correct as far as it goes; but on the present facts, the **mortgage documents plausibly are** that strict compliance:

- They are written.  
- They are signed by persons authorised to act for JEV.  
- They are relied upon by JEV as confirmation of EPF’s beneficial title.

Steel Horizon’s attempt to invalidate the trust because the signatories were “merely agents” is weak in company law terms and contrary to usual practice in applying s 53(1)(b) to corporate landowners.

### (c) “Mortgage documents are weak evidence of beneficial ownership”

They may not be *ideal*, but the statute does not insist on a formal trust deed. The test is whether the writing **“manifests and proves”** the trust—i.e. whether it evidences, with sufficient clarity, that JEV holds the property beneficially for EPF.

If, as JEV claims, these documents do just that, a court is likely to treat them as adequate written evidence.

### (d) Policy and section 423’s protective purpose

Section 423 is certainly aimed at preventing fraudulent conveyances and abusive undervalue transactions. But it is **not** a free-standing power to disregard genuine trusts simply because their timing is unfortunate from a creditor’s point of view.

To let Steel Horizon succeed here, the court would effectively have to:

- Disregard a trust that is properly evidenced under s 53(1)(b), and  
- Treat bare legal title in a nominee as if it were part of the debtor’s beneficial estate.

That would cut across settled trust principles and would expose many nominee, pension and custodial structures to creditor claims in ways Parliament has not provided for.

---

## 7. Conclusion

On the legal framework and the facts provided:

- The mortgage-related documents are capable of satisfying the requirement in s 53(1)(b) LPA 1925 that the trust be “manifested and proved” in writing signed by a person able to declare the trust.  
- As a corporate owner, JEV can properly manifest and prove the trust through documents signed by its authorised representatives.  
- Once that is accepted, EPF is recognised as the beneficial owner at all material times; JEV held only bare legal title.  
- The eventual transfer of that legal title to EPF does not amount to a transaction at an undervalue for s 423 purposes, because JEV never had any beneficial asset to dispose of.  
- Steel Horizon’s suspicions about timing and intent are understandable but cannot enlarge s 423 to reach property that was never beneficially JEV’s.

Accordingly, **Jade Energy Ventures** should prevail, and Steel Horizon’s section 423 claim should fail.
