## 1. The legal test under the Part‑time Workers Regulations

The key provisions are in the Part‑time Workers (Prevention of Less Favourable Treatment) Regulations 2000 (“the Regulations”), which implement the Framework Agreement annexed to Directive 97/81/EC.

Broadly, a claimant must show:

1. He is a “part‑time worker” within the meaning of the Regulations (accepted here).
2. He has an actual full‑time comparator who is a “comparable full‑time worker” (same employer, same or broadly similar work, etc.).
3. He has been treated less favourably than that comparator **“by reason of the fact” that he is a part‑time worker** (reg 5(2)); this is the “on the ground of” causation issue.
4. If 1–3 are established, the employer can only succeed if it shows the treatment is justified on objective grounds (reg 5(2)(b), 5(3)).

The phrase “by reason of the fact that” mirrors the “on the grounds of” language used for discrimination more generally. Case law on discrimination (e.g. *Nagarajan v London Regional Transport* [1999] and subsequent authorities) establishes that:

- The protected ground **need not be the sole or even the principal reason**.
- It must, however, be an **effective and operative cause** of the treatment.

So Reeves does **not** have to prove that his part‑time status was the only reason. He must show it was one of the material reasons why he was treated as he was.

The dispute is whether that effective causal nexus exists here.

---

## 2. Is there “less favourable treatment” at all?

### (a) Identification of the treatment

The treatment complained of is the **requirement to pay a flat “circuit fee”** in order to access the booking system.

This fee is:

- The same amount for every driver,
- Charged on the same basis,
- Regardless of whether the driver is part‑time or full‑time.

On its face, there is no explicit contractual term that says: “part‑time workers must pay more / are subject to a fee which full‑time workers do not pay.” The term is facially neutral and universal.

### (b) Appropriate comparator

The proper comparator is:

- a full‑time driver employed by Stone Rides,
- doing the same or similar driving work,
- paying the **same flat fee for the same access** to the booking system.

On a straightforward reading, both Reeves and a full‑time comparator are subject to **identical contractual obligations** on this point.

### (c) What counts as “less favourable”?

Under the Regulations (and the Directive), what matters is whether the part‑time worker has **less favourable terms or conditions of employment**, *taken as such*, by comparison with the full‑time worker, not whether an otherwise neutral term bites harder in practice because of how the worker chooses or is constrained to work.

Here:

- The **term itself** is the same.
- The **practical economic effect** differs because part‑time drivers spread a fixed cost over fewer hours or fewer rides.

That difference in outcome arises from different **levels of utilisation** of the same facility, not from any difference in the term itself. The Regulations are aimed at **disparities in contractual treatment** *because of part‑time status*, not at ensuring that every neutral cost is perfectly proportionate to hours worked.

If a uniform, neutral charge that everyone pays counts as “less favourable treatment” simply because less‑used workers derive less benefit per pound paid, the protections for part‑time workers would effectively become:

- A general proportionality review of any flat fee or fixed cost in employment,
- Even where there is **no differential treatment in the contract**.

That is not how the Framework Agreement has been interpreted. The CJEU, in the part‑time workers line of cases (e.g. *Wippel*, *Del Cerro Alonso*), focuses on ensuring that **differences in treatment between part‑ and full‑time staff** are justified, not on requiring employers to calibrate all neutral terms to hours worked.

On a proper construction, the better view is that Reeves has **not** suffered “less favourable treatment” in terms of the contractual obligation itself: he and a full‑time comparator have the same obligation to pay the same fee.

---

## 3. Causation: is the fee “on the ground” of part‑time status?

Assuming for argument’s sake that the net effect on Reeves can be characterised as “less favourable”, he must still show that this treatment was **“on the ground”** of his being a part‑time worker, i.e.:

- That his part‑time status was an effective causal reason for the imposition of the fee, not merely a background fact.

### (a) The employer’s reason

The findings you’ve set out indicate that:

- Stone Rides imposed the circuit fee on **all drivers**.
- The reason advanced is a **commercial one**: generating revenue in line with industry practice where the operator does not itself collect customer fares.

On those facts, the **operative reason** for the fee is:

- “You are a driver using our booking system; we need to fund the platform; everyone in that position pays a fee,”
- Not “you are part‑time, therefore you must pay (or you must pay an amount that is relatively worse for you).”

### (b) Reeves’ argument: disproportionate impact and “significant factor”

Reeves’ main contention is not that the fee is explicitly tied to his part‑time status, but that:

- The **structure** of the fee (being flat, not pro‑rated) **disproportionately harms part‑timers**, because they have less work over which to spread the fixed cost.
- Therefore, his part‑time status is a **significant reason** why he is adversely affected.

That is essentially an *indirect discrimination*‑type argument: a neutral provision has a disparate impact on a protected group.

But the legal regime we are dealing with here is not the Equality Act’s indirect discrimination test; it is the specific part‑time workers regime, framed in terms of **less favourable treatment “by reason of the fact” that the worker is part‑time**, coupled with a justification defence.

For this framework, the mere fact that:

- A neutral term has a **disproportionate economic effect** on part‑timers,
- Without evidence that the employer adopted or maintained the rule **because it was part‑timers who would be affected**,

is not enough to establish that the treatment is **“on the ground”** of part‑time status. The protected ground must be part of the employer’s **reasons for the term**, not just part of the employee’s circumstances that make the term feel harsher.

Thus:

- Reeves is correct in principle that part‑time status need not be the **sole** reason.
- But he still needs to show it was one of the **effective reasons** why the employer imposed the fee, not just that he feels the consequences more acutely.

On the stated facts, there is no indication that Stone Rides adopted the flat fee *because* of any view about part‑time drivers, or to treat them worse; the fee was levied identically on all drivers for a revenue‑raising purpose.

That is a **legitimate, status‑neutral reason**, and there is no evidence that part‑time status played any role at all, let alone a material one, in the decision to impose the fee or to set it at that level.

---

## 4. Objective justification (if needed)

Even if the court were persuaded, contrary to the analysis above, that:

- there was “less favourable treatment” because the net effect on Reeves was worse; and
- it could be loosely said to be “by reason of” his part‑time status (on a broad reading that treats disparate impact as enough),

Stone Rides would still have a strong case on **objective justification** under reg 5(2)(b) and 5(3):

- **Legitimate aim**: funding the booking platform where the operator does not collect fares, in line with industry practice, is plainly legitimate.
- **Appropriateness**: a flat fee for access to the system is a straightforward, transparent way to achieve that aim.
- **Necessity / Proportionality**: unless there is evidence that a materially less intrusive structure (e.g. purely percentage‑based commissions) is viable in the sector and would have been reasonably practicable for this employer, a court is likely to accept the flat fee as a proportionate business arrangement.

Given:

- the universality of the scheme,
- the lack of any targeted detriment to part‑timers,
- and the commercial justification,

Stone Rides’ fee system is highly likely to be seen as objectively justified in any event.

---

## 5. Comparison with Directive 97/81 and its purpose

The Directive and Framework Agreement are designed to:

- Prevent employers from treating part‑time workers worse **as part‑time workers**,
- Unless that difference is justified on objective grounds.

They do not go so far as to require that:

- Every employment‑related cost must be arithmetically proportionate to working hours, or
- Employers re‑design every neutral term that might, in practice, be costlier per hour for some staff than others.

If the court accepted Reeves’ theory, then any **fixed cost** (e.g. uniform subscription to a training portal, parking pass, licence fee, or union‑negotiated levy) would potentially be unlawful for part‑timers, simply because they make fewer uses of the underlying facility. That would overshoot the Directive’s purpose and effectively convert it into a general equalisation/pro‑rata review of all fixed costs, which neither the text nor the case law supports.

Interpreting “on the ground of” as requiring a **real causal connection** between part‑time status and the employer’s decision maintains coherence with wider EU and UK discrimination law, while still catching cases where an employer **does** in substance adopt terms that disadvantage part‑timers because of how little they work.

---

## 6. Overall conclusion

- Reeves does not need to show that part‑time status was the **sole** cause, but he does need to show it was an **effective reason** for the treatment.
- On the facts, the only operative reason for the fee is a **status‑neutral commercial rationale**, applied identically to part‑time and full‑time drivers.
- The contractual term itself is the same for both; the worse “per‑hour” outcome for part‑timers arises from their lower use of the system, not from different treatment *as workers*.
- Even if one strained to find “less favourable treatment” and a causal link, the arrangement would be objectively justified.

An English court, interpreting the Regulations consistently with Directive 97/81 and existing discrimination principles, should therefore conclude that Reeves has not been treated less favourably “on the ground” of being a part‑time worker.

The tribunal’s task is to decide, on the lower standard of proof (“reasonable degree of likelihood”), whether Mr. Ho has a well‑founded fear of persecution for a Refugee Convention reason or faces a real risk of serious harm on return (for humanitarian protection), taking account of credibility, corroboration, timing and general country conditions. Section 8 of the Asylum and Immigration (Treatment of Claimants, etc.) Act 2004 is part of that assessment, not a standalone ground for refusal.

I’ll go through the key issues in turn.

---

## 1. Legal framework and issues

To succeed in an asylum claim Mr. Ho must show:

1. A **well‑founded fear of persecution** (i.e. serious harm) in Vietnam;
2. **For a Convention reason** (race, religion, nationality, political opinion, or membership of a particular social group);
3. **By the state or by non‑state actors whom the state is unable or unwilling to control**; and
4. That he **cannot reasonably obtain protection elsewhere in the country or relocate internally**.

For **humanitarian protection** / Article 3 ECHR, he must show a real risk of serious harm on return, irrespective of Convention reasons, but still tied to future risk and availability of protection.

The main factual disputes are:

- Whether his story of extortion and assaults around military‑service exemption is broadly true;
- Whether the assaults amount to persecution / serious harm;
- Whether they are linked to a Convention ground (e.g. imputed political opinion, or membership of a particular social group such as “relatives of martyrs” or “those resisting corrupt officials”);
- Whether the Vietnamese authorities are unwilling or unable to protect him or whether internal relocation would be reasonable.

---

## 2. Credibility of Mr. Ho’s core account

### 2.1 Medical evidence

Mr. Ho has two medical reports from River Clinic and Maple District Hospital in Ho Chi Minh City showing injuries. These:

- Support the fact that he **suffered physical harm** at around the dates claimed.
- Do **not** conclusively establish *who* inflicted those injuries or *why*.

Key credibility concern: he gave different explanations for the injuries to hospital staff than he now gives for the asylum claim. His explanation is that he feared retaliation if the true cause were recorded.

An English tribunal typically assesses this as follows:

- Victims of violence often give **incomplete or misleading explanations** to local professionals where they fear the aggressors are connected to, or can influence, the authorities. This is recognised in asylum jurisprudence. So the mere inconsistency does not automatically destroy credibility.
- But equally, **this inconsistency means the reports cannot be read as contemporaneous corroboration of persecution**. They corroborate trauma, not its persecutory motive or source.

Net effect: the medical evidence helps only with the limited proposition that he sustained non‑trivial injuries. It does **not strongly corroborate the persecution narrative**.

### 2.2 The military‑service exemption

The Secretary of State relies on official documentation recording that:

- Mr. Ho’s father had “martyr” status; and
- That status gives Mr. Ho an exemption from compulsory military service.

If trustworthy, that documentation **directly undercuts the proposition** that he was legitimately pursued for failing to perform military service. Mr. Ho’s case then becomes: he was not actually liable to serve, but **corrupt officials still tried to extort him by pretending he was**.

That scenario is possible in principle. But it creates a key difficulty:

- The **core factual matrix of risk** is now entirely dependent on the assertion that specific local actors disregarded official records and used the exemption status itself as leverage for extortion.
- There is no independent corroboration of who these actors were, their official capacity (if any), or any formal steps they took that could be cross‑checked (e.g. fraudulent call‑up papers, summonses).

An English tribunal would likely hold: the official document is strong, objective evidence that there was **no lawful basis** for any state‑driven enforcement of service. That doesn’t *disprove* extortion, but it increases the need for **detailed, coherent, consistent** evidence about the alleged corruption. On the outline given, Mr. Ho’s account seems high‑level (“they demanded annual bribes”) without granular details about individuals, dates, specific threats, or attempts at remedy that can be tested.

On balance, **the documentation is more persuasive than the uncorroborated allegation of extortion**, and it undermines the central plank of his claim.

### 2.3 Lack of corroboration and conduct in Vietnam

Mr. Ho:

- Produced no evidence of **payments** (which is common in extortion cases, but here the tribunal would at least expect a clear, consistent, detailed narrative of amounts, frequency, and circumstances).
- Made no complaints to Vietnamese authorities or higher‑level officials, or at least provides no evidence of any attempts to seek redress or protection.

In an asylum context, failure to complain is not automatically detrimental because victims may reasonably fear state complicity. But where:

- The alleged persecutors are said to be **state‑linked** (e.g. local officials) yet:
- The **central government’s official records** clearly reflect his exemption status, and
- There is no attempt even to approach **higher or alternative organs of the state** or to relocate internally,

a tribunal is likely to find that **the assertion of total futility or danger in seeking protection is not sufficiently evidenced**.

The absence of any contemporaneous steps consistent with someone facing repeated yearly extortion and serious assaults will weigh against him, even allowing for fear and corruption.

### 2.4 Delay and manner of claiming protection (Section 8)

Section 8 of the 2004 Act requires the tribunal to treat certain behaviour as damaging to credibility where appropriate. Relevant here:

- Mr. Ho absconded from his ship.
- He remained unlawfully.
- He engaged in serious criminality (cannabis production).
- He **did not claim asylum** or seek protection until **after deportation action was initiated** following his conviction.

Courts have repeatedly held that:

- Late claims and opportunistic behaviour are **not determinative**, but are **weighing factors** that may undermine credibility (R v Asylum and Immigration Tribunal, ex p YH [2010], and others).
- The tribunal must still look at the substance of the risk and cannot treat Section 8 as a trump card.

Here, the sequence—illegal stay, serious crime, only then a protection claim—will be treated as **strongly suggestive** of a tactical, manufactured narrative. Any innocent explanation he offers (fear, lack of knowledge of the system, mistrust of authorities) must be weighed, but in light of his criminal involvement and long silence in the UK, a tribunal is likely to find those explanations unconvincing.

The fact that he was prepared to **engage with criminal networks** in the UK undercuts any claim that his fear of authorities was so overpowering that he could not possibly raise his situation earlier.

### 2.5 Overall credibility

Putting this together, the tribunal will likely conclude:

- Some harm occurred in Vietnam (medical evidence).
- But the **link** between that harm and the alleged long‑running military‑service‑related extortion by state‑linked actors is **not established to the lower standard**, given:
  - Strong contrary official evidence about military exemption;
  - Lack of specific, detailed, internally consistent testimony;
  - Lack of any plausible supporting documentary or witness evidence;
  - Total failure to seek any kind of higher‑level protection or relocation within Vietnam;
  - And highly adverse inferences under Section 8 from his late, post‑conviction asylum claim.

Accordingly, his *core account of persecution* is likely to be found not credible.

---

## 3. Even assuming some aspects of his story, is there a Refugee Convention nexus?

Even if the tribunal were to accept that:

- Local officials demanded bribes; and
- Assaulted him when he did not (or could not) pay,

there remains the issue of **Convention nexus**.

The claim as presented is essentially that he was:

- A victim of **corruption and criminal extortion**, not of persecution for race, religion, nationality, political opinion, or membership of a particular social group.

Arguments could be attempted:

- **Imputed political opinion**: refusal to comply with extortion by state agents could be interpreted as opposition to the authorities. But there is no evidence that he was targeted for political beliefs or opposition; the motive appears purely financial.
- **Particular social group**: “children of martyrs” or “people exempted from service” might arguably form a recognisable group, but the evidence here is that his status should protect him; the alleged mistreatment arises from opportunism, not targeting of that group generally.

UK case law generally treats **economic extortion by corrupt officials**, motivated by personal financial gain, as not engaging the Refugee Convention unless there is clear evidence that the harm is inflicted “for reason of” a Convention ground. On the facts as provided, the more convincing interpretation is that he was (on his own case) targeted *because he was seen as someone from whom money could be extracted*, not because of who he is in Convention terms.

So even if some part of his story is believed, **he would struggle to meet the Refugee Convention ground requirement**.

---

## 4. State protection and internal relocation

To obtain either asylum or humanitarian protection, there must be:

- A real risk of future serious harm; and
- Either **absence of effective state protection** or **impracticability of internal relocation**.

On the evidence:

- Central records show his exemption from military service, suggesting that **where properly applied, the legal system protects** him from conscription.
- He has provided **no credible evidence** that he attempted to rely on those legal protections by going above the local level, nor that central or alternative authorities were complicit.
- Vietnam is a large country with multiple regions; there is nothing in his account (e.g. national‑level blacklisting, high‑profile opposition activity) suggesting he could not **safely relocate to another area** away from the particular corrupt officials.

A tribunal is likely to find that:

- Even if there were problems with some local actors, **sufficiency of protection** is available from the Vietnamese state overall; or
- At minimum, **internal relocation** is a reasonable and effective alternative.

That conclusion is reinforced by the lack of evidence of wider, country‑wide persecution of individuals in his position.

---

## 5. Impact of criminal conduct on outcome

His conviction for cannabis production is not itself decisive on whether he has protection needs, but:

- It **weakens his personal credibility**, especially in combination with late claim and illegal residence.
- In terms of the overall proportionality and public interest (particularly under Article 8 ECHR in deportation appeals), it weighs heavily against him.
- Since his asylum/humanitarian protection claim is already weak on credibility, nexus, and protection, the criminality does not “tip” a marginal protection claim over the line; instead it adds to the reasons to uphold deportation.

If, hypothetically, he had strong, well‑supported evidence of a real risk of Article 3 ill‑treatment, the criminal offending could not justify return. But here, on the facts, **the risk itself is not made out**.

---

## 6. Section 8 and the overall standard of proof

The tribunal must not treat Section 8 as automatically fatal. It must still ask:

- Is there a **real risk** (not probability) that his account of persecution is true?

But weighing:

- The adverse Section 8 factors (late claim, absconding, criminality);
- The strength of official documentation on exemption;
- The weakness of corroboration on extortion and motive;
- The plausible availability of state protection and internal relocation;

an English tribunal is likely to find Mr. Ho has **not discharged even the lower standard of proof** that he would face a real risk of persecution or serious harm on return.

---

## 7. Conclusion

On a careful, stepwise application of UK asylum and human rights law to the facts as presented:

- His **core account** of being persecuted over military‑service exemption and bribes is not sufficiently credible;
- Even if partly true, it does not strongly engage a **Convention reason** but instead reflects ordinary (albeit serious) corruption and criminality;
- There is insufficient evidence that **state protection is unavailable** or that internal relocation in Vietnam would be unreasonable;
- Section 8 considerations and his criminal conduct significantly undermine, rather than support, his claim.

Accordingly, the Secretary of State’s refusal of asylum and decision to deport would, on these facts, properly be upheld.

Under the Part-time Workers (Prevention of Less Favourable Treatment) Regulations 2000 (“the Regulations”), Stone Rides Inc. is prohibited from treating a part-time worker less favourably than a comparable full-time worker as regards terms of employment “on the ground that” he is a part-time worker (reg 5).

The issues are:

1. What “on the ground that” means in causation terms (sole cause vs one effective cause); and  
2. Whether the circuit fee constitutes less favourable treatment of Mr Reeves as a part-time worker, and, if so, whether it is objectively justified.

---

### 1. Causation: does part-time status need to be the sole reason?

The company’s submission that Mr Reeves must show his part-time status was the *sole* ground of the impugned treatment is not consistent with general UK or EU discrimination principles, nor with the structure and purpose of the Regulations and Directive 97/81.

#### (a) General approach in UK discrimination law

In discrimination law, the test is whether the protected ground was **a** cause or operative reason, not the sole or even main cause. The House of Lords in *Nagarajan v London Regional Transport* made this clear in the context of race discrimination: the protected characteristic need only be “a reason why” the claimant was treated as he was, not “the reason”. That approach has been repeated in subsequent discrimination decisions under later legislation.

The Regulations implement EU Directive 97/81, which itself is an anti-discrimination measure. There is no basis in the Directive for a stricter, “sole cause” standard. To the contrary, EU discrimination law consistently treats protected grounds as needing only to be an effective or operative cause among others.

#### (b) Text and purpose of the Regulations and Directive

- The UK Regulations use “on the ground that” the worker is part-time;  
- The Directive’s purpose is to prevent **discrimination against part-time workers** and to “improve the quality of part-time work” and remove unjustified disadvantages.

If “on the ground that” were read as “only if part-time status is the sole cause,” the protection would be hollow. Almost any disadvantageous policy can be characterised as driven partly by cost-saving, revenue generation, administrative convenience, or “sector norms”. If the presence of such ancillary reasons automatically defeated a claim, the Regulations would be easily circumvented.

A court interpreting UK law in conformity with the Directive would reject such a narrow reading. The coherent approach is:

- The claimant must show that, **but for his part-time status**, he would not have been treated less favourably than a comparable full-time worker, or that his part‑time status was a real and effective reason why the treatment applied as it did to him (or to part-timers as a class);  
- It is **not** necessary that it be the only reason.

Here, both sides accept that Mr Reeves’ part-time status was “a factor” in his treatment. That is enough to cross the causation threshold, subject to the employer’s justification defence.

---

### 2. Is there “less favourable treatment” as a part-time worker?

Regulation 5 prohibits less favourable treatment of a part‑time worker “as regards the terms of his contract or any … benefit” where that is on the ground that he is part-time, unless objectively justified.

#### (a) Comparator and nature of the term

- All drivers (part-time and full-time) pay the same flat “circuit fee” to access the booking system.  
- A comparable full-time worker is another driver doing the same or broadly similar work on more hours for the same employer.

The fee is a term or condition imposed uniformly in form. The crucial question is: does it result in the part-time worker being placed in a less favourable position than the full-time comparator?

#### (b) Economic impact on part-time vs full-time workers

On the facts as presented, the fee is fixed. Its economic burden is clearly heavier for part-time drivers:

- For a full-time driver, the fee might equate to (for example) 5% of weekly or monthly earnings;  
- For a part-time driver like Mr Reeves, working substantially fewer hours and earning less, it might represent 15% or more of earnings.

Thus, although the fee is the same nominally, the **relative detriment** is greater for part-time workers. What matters under the Regulations is not only whether the literal contractual term is identical, but whether the part-time worker is treated less favourably *in substance* as regards terms, compared with the full-time worker.

That is consistent with the protective purpose of the Directive: formally equal terms that systematically burden part-time workers more heavily can amount to less favourable treatment of part‑timers as a class.

On these facts, a court should be prepared to find that Mr Reeves is subject to less favourable treatment in relation to pay/benefits than his full-time comparators, arising from the way the fee operates.

---

### 3. Causation applied to these facts

Given that both parties agree part-time status was “a factor”:

- The company cannot credibly say the difference in effect on part-time workers is entirely irrelevant to why the scheme exists as it does. The scheme is designed against a background in which some workers do many hours and some do few, and its cost-distribution consequences were knowable and (in discrimination terms) attributable to the employer.  
- Once it is accepted that being part-time was one operative reason why Mr Reeves was worse off under the scheme than comparable full-time drivers, the causation limb (“on the ground that he is a part-time worker”) is met.

The company’s reliance on revenue generation and sector norms goes to **justification**, not to whether part-time status was a relevant cause.

---

### 4. Objective justification

Even where there is less favourable treatment on the ground of part-time status, regulation 5(2) allows the employer to justify it if the treatment is:

- Pursuing a **legitimate objective**, and  
- **Appropriate and necessary** (proportionate) to achieving that objective.

#### (a) Legitimate aim

Stone Rides Inc. can plausibly advance legitimate aims:

- Generating revenue to fund and maintain the booking system;  
- Aligning with sector norms;  
- Administrative simplicity in charging a standard fee.

Those are the kinds of aims that tribunals often accept as legitimate.

#### (b) Proportionality assessment

The decisive question is whether a **flat, non‑pro‑rated circuit fee** is a proportionate way of achieving those aims, given:

- Its significantly greater financial impact on part-time workers;  
- The availability (at least conceptually) of **less discriminatory alternatives**, such as:
  - A percentage-of-earnings fee;  
  - A fee per booking;  
  - A tiered fee based on typical hours or income bands; or  
  - A reduced fee for part-time workers, so their relative burden is no worse than that of full-time drivers.

If other methods could achieve the revenue aim while distributing the burden more evenly between full-time and part-time staff, a flat fee will struggle to be justified.

Stone Rides Inc.’s argument focuses mainly on the existence of a business rationale and sector norms. That is **not enough**: in discrimination law, cost and convenience alone rarely justify a practice that disproportionately disadvantages a protected category. The employer must show:

- Why a uniform flat fee is **necessary**, as opposed to merely easier;  
- Why alternatives with less adverse impact on part-timers would fail to meet the legitimate aim or be unduly burdensome.

On the facts given, there is no indication that Stone Rides Inc. has such evidence. The justification advanced (revenue and norms) explains *why* the scheme exists, but not *why it must take this particular, more burdensome form* for part‑time drivers.

Given that other, more proportionate structures are clearly conceivable and used in other sectors (e.g. commission-based or usage-based contributions), a court is unlikely to find a flat, non-adjusted fee proportionate where it predictably places a heavier financial strain on part-time workers.

---

### 5. Conclusion

Legally, the better analysis is:

- “On the ground” of part-time status **does not require** sole causation; being an effective or material cause is enough.  
- Here, part-time status is accepted as a factor and is linked to a clear relative detriment when compared with full-time drivers.  
- The circuit fee therefore results in less favourable treatment of Mr Reeves as a part-time worker under reg 5.  
- Stone Rides Inc.’s justifications (revenue and sector norms), without more, are insufficient to establish that a flat, identical fee—despite its disparate impact—is a necessary and proportionate way of achieving those aims.

On the law and the stated facts, an English court should find for the claimant.

Avalon Reeves

The crucial question is whether, at the time of the impugned transfer, Iris House was genuinely part of Jade Energy Ventures’ beneficial estate or was already held on trust for Emerald Pension Fund (“EPF”). If it was already trust property, there was no “transaction at an undervalue” for section 423 Insolvency Act 1986 purposes.

I’ll go through the key issues step by step.

---

## 1. Structure of a section 423 Insolvency Act 1986 claim

For Steel Horizon to succeed under section 423, it must show:

1. Jade entered into a “transaction” which included a gift or a transfer for no (or significantly less) consideration, i.e. a “transaction at an undervalue”; and  
2. Jade did so for the purpose of putting assets beyond the reach of its creditors or otherwise prejudicing their interests.

The timing of the transfer—shortly after Steel Horizon obtained permission to enforce the arbitral award—is strongly indicative of the required purpose. If Iris House were Jade’s asset, the requisite intent would almost certainly be inferred.

The real battleground is therefore the first limb: was there a disposition of Jade’s own beneficial property, or was Jade merely transferring bare legal title to EPF?

---

## 2. Did Jade beneficially own Iris House?

### 2.1. The alleged trust in favour of EPF

Jade’s case is that:

- EPF was at all times the true beneficial owner, in the context of a pension arrangement; and  
- Jade held only the legal title, as trustee for EPF.

If that is right, then Jade’s act in transferring the registered title to EPF is just a trustee transferring legal title to the beneficiary. That does not deplete the trustee’s own beneficial estate and so is not a “transaction at an undervalue” for section 423.

So everything turns on whether a valid trust of the land was created and properly evidenced in compliance with section 53(1)(b) of the Law of Property Act 1925.

---

## 3. Section 53(1)(b) LPA 1925 – what does it actually require?

Section 53(1)(b) provides:

> A declaration of trust respecting any land or any interest therein must be **manifested and proved by some writing** signed by some person who **is able to declare such trust** or by his will.

Key points from the wording and the case law:

1. The trust itself may be oral; section 53(1)(b) is an **evidential** requirement. The declaration of trust must be “manifested and proved” in writing; the writing can come later.  
2. The writing need not be a formal “trust deed” or contain any particular formula; clear written acknowledgement of the trust will suffice.  
3. The signature must be by a person “able to declare such trust” – i.e. the person in whom the relevant beneficial interest is vested at the time (here, Jade as legal and beneficial owner when the trust was declared).  
4. In general, a company acts through its authorised officers and agents; their signatures, done with actual or ostensible authority, are legally treated as the company’s own act.

There is nothing in the wording of section 53(1)(b) that requires the “landowner’s own hand” in a personal sense, as opposed to a signature affixed by an authorised signatory. English law routinely accepts that where a statute requires signature by a person, that act can be done by an agent unless the statute expressly provides otherwise.

---

## 4. Do the mortgage documents satisfy s.53(1)(b)?

On the facts given, the two mortgage-related documents:

- are in writing;  
- expressly identify EPF as the beneficial owner of Iris House; and  
- are signed by representatives of Jade, acting in that capacity.

Assuming (as nothing suggests otherwise) that these representatives were duly authorised officers/agents of Jade, their signatures are the signatures of the “person who is able to declare such trust” for the purposes of section 53(1)(b). That is how companies must, as a matter of practical and legal necessity, express their intentions.

Steel Horizon’s argument that the landowner “itself” did not sign misunderstands corporate personality and agency. A company can only “sign” through humans. Provided the representatives had authority to sign documents relating to Jade’s property or financing, their signatures are sufficient.

Moreover, the documents do more than contain a vague or gratuitous statement; they:

- describe Iris House as belonging beneficially to EPF; and  
- are used in connection with mortgage/financing arrangements in which the property is treated as an asset of EPF.

Taken together, that is powerful, objective evidence that Jade had already declared or acknowledged that it held Iris House on trust for EPF.

Section 53(1)(b) is satisfied if the declaration of trust is “manifested and proved” by such writing; the statute does not insist that the same document both creates and evidences the trust, nor that the document be designed *primarily* as a trust instrument.

---

## 5. Policy and equity: using formalities to defeat, or to facilitate, trust arrangements

From an equitable perspective, the court will be slow to allow a formalities provision to be manipulated so as to:

- disregard a clearly evidenced, long‑standing pension trust; and  
- permit general creditors to invade pension assets that commercial practice has consistently treated as ring‑fenced for beneficiaries.

Equity has long been wary of using formalities as an “instrument of fraud.” Where there is written, signed, contemporaneous documentation treating EPF as beneficial owner, it would be artificial to treat Iris House as genuinely part of Jade’s own estate just because the written acknowledgment happened to be embedded in mortgage documents rather than in a document labelled “Declaration of Trust.”

Here the commercial reality (a property held in connection with a pension arrangement, with filings and mortgage documents reflecting EPF’s beneficial ownership) aligns with the legal formalities. That is precisely the kind of situation in which courts are inclined to recognise and give effect to the trust.

---

## 6. Consequence for section 423

If Iris House was already held on trust for EPF:

- Jade’s “asset” in Iris House was only the bare legal title.  
- The transfer of that legal title to EPF did not deprive Jade of any beneficial interest.  
- Therefore there was no “transaction at an undervalue” within section 423, because Jade did not dispose of its own beneficial property at an undervalue; it was simply performing its duty as trustee.

The timing and potential intent to prejudice creditors become largely irrelevant once it is accepted that the property was not Jade’s in the first place, in beneficial terms. Section 423 is not a vehicle to reorder the beneficial ownership of trust property or to treat trust assets as if they belonged beneficially to the debtor.

---

## 7. Conclusion

On these facts, a court applying orthodox principles of trust law and corporate agency should find that:

- The mortgage-related documents constitute written, signed acknowledgment by Jade (via its authorised representatives) that EPF was the beneficial owner of Iris House;  
- That writing is sufficient to “manifest and prove” a trust for the purposes of section 53(1)(b) LPA 1925;  
- Consequently, Iris House was held on trust for EPF and was not beneficially part of Jade’s estate; and  
- The subsequent transfer of legal title to EPF did not constitute a “transaction at an undervalue” under section 423 IA 1986.

The section 423 claim should therefore fail, and Jade Energy Ventures should prevail.

Jade Energy Ventures

1. **Legal framework**

   a. **Refugee status**

   Mr. Ho must show a “well‑founded fear of being persecuted” in Vietnam for a Refugee Convention reason (race, religion, nationality, political opinion, or membership of a particular social group), and that the Vietnamese state is unable or unwilling to provide him with protection (Refugee Convention; *Ravichandran* [1996] Imm AR 97; Qualification Regulations).

   The standard of proof is “a reasonable degree of likelihood” / “real risk” (*Karanakaran* [2000] EWCA Civ 11).

   b. **Humanitarian protection / Article 3 ECHR**

   Even if no Convention reason is established, he could still succeed on humanitarian protection / Article 3 ECHR if there is a real risk of serious harm on return from state or non‑state actors, and adequate state protection is not available (see *Horvath* [2000] UKHL 37; *Bagdanavicius* [2005] UKHL 38).

   c. **Credibility and delay – Asylum and Immigration (Treatment of Claimants, etc.) Act 2004**

   Section 8 requires the tribunal to take into account, as damaging to credibility, behaviour such as:
   - Failure to claim asylum promptly; and
   - Making a claim only once enforcement action is in train; and
   - Inconsistent accounts.

   It does **not** require that the claim be dismissed because of such behaviour, but it directs the fact‑finder to treat it as adverse when assessing credibility.

   d. **Corroboration**

   Asylum claims do not require corroboration as a matter of law, but the tribunal is entitled to give less weight to uncorroborated accounts, especially where the account is implausible or inconsistent. Documents are assessed under the approach in *Tanveer Ahmed* [2002] UKIAT 00439: it is for the claimant to show that a document is reliable; a document does not automatically prove the facts it asserts.

2. **Issues to be determined**

   1. Is Mr. Ho’s core account (extortion and assaults relating to military service exemption and his father’s martyr status) **credible**?
   2. Is there a **real risk of serious harm** on return to Vietnam from the same or similar actors?
   3. If so, is there a **Convention reason** or, failing that, does he at least satisfy humanitarian protection / Article 3?
   4. Is there **sufficient state protection** or a realistic internal relocation option?
   5. How should the **delay and inconsistencies** be weighed under the 2004 Act?

3. **Credibility analysis**

   a. **Delay in claiming asylum**

   - He only advanced a protection claim after he had been served with notice of intention to deport.
   - This is squarely within s.8 behaviour: a late “opportunistic” claim to avoid removal.
   - His explanation – that he did not trust authorities due to corruption – is possible, but:
     - He was content to work in the UK and engage with UK authorities in the criminal process.
     - He did not mention any fear of return during the criminal proceedings or immediately after arrest.
   - An English court / tribunal is likely to treat the delay as **significantly damaging** to his credibility, while accepting it is not determinative.

   b. **Inconsistency about the cause of injuries**

   - Medical records from River Clinic and Maple District Hospital show injuries consistent with assault.
   - However, his own case is that he **deliberately gave false explanations** for the cause of those injuries to medical staff.
   - A tribunal is likely to reason:
     - The fact of injury is supported, but
     - The provenance of the injuries hinges on his credibility, because the **only direct evidence of who caused the injuries is his oral account**.
   - The explanation – fear of the aggressors’ influence – is not inherently implausible, but it does have consequences: if he chose to mislead medical staff before, the tribunal is entitled to be cautious about taking his current explanation at face value.
   - Thus the medical evidence is **neutral to mildly supportive** (showing he was assaulted by someone) but does **not** directly corroborate that the assaults were linked to a bribe/extortion scheme over military service.

   c. **Military service and martyr status**

   - The Secretary of State relies on official Vietnamese documents showing that his father’s martyr status exempts Mr. Ho from military service.
   - Mr. Ho’s own case is not that the law required him to serve, but that corrupt individuals ignored the law and extorted him anyway.
   - That is logically possible, but:
     - It reduces the connection between his problems and any formal military obligation; and
     - It makes his account dependent on a specific, localised pattern of corruption and extortion which he has **not corroborated** by independent country evidence or documents.
   - An English tribunal would likely:
     - Accept that corruption exists in Vietnam generally, but
     - Find that Mr. Ho has **not produced objective evidence** that people in his particular circumstances (children of martyrs exempt from conscription) are commonly extorted, nor that this happened to him specifically.
   - In line with *Tanveer Ahmed*, the existence of official documents about the exemption undercuts the plausibility that military authorities had any legitimate leverage over him; the extortion story then depends heavily on his unsupported word.

   d. **Lack of complaint or attempt to seek protection**

   - Mr. Ho never made any complaint to Vietnamese authorities, nor any effort to seek protection.
   - Where the alleged persecutors are non‑state actors or corrupt individuals acting outside the law, *Horvath* and *Bagdanavicius* require careful consideration of state protection:
     - Generally, the claimant must at least attempt to seek protection, unless there is cogent country evidence showing such attempts would be futile or dangerous.
   - His explanation – that these individuals had local influence and he feared retaliation – is again possible, but:
     - There is no evidence before the court that complaints against military or local officials in his area are systematically futile, or that victims are typically punished for seeking help.
     - In the absence of such evidence, the tribunal is unlikely to infer that any attempt at state protection would have been useless.
   - The complete absence of any approach to the authorities **undermines both credibility and the claim that the state cannot or will not protect him**.

   e. **Overall credibility**

   Taking all of the above together, and applying the lower “real risk” standard:

   - Factors damaging credibility (which the tribunal is required by the 2004 Act to take into account):
     - Late asylum claim only after deportation action.
     - Admitted prior dishonesty to medical staff about cause of injuries.
     - Lack of corroboration of the extortion/bribe narrative.
     - No approach to local or national authorities, despite the alleged seriousness and recurrence of the threats.
   - Factors supportive of his account:
     - Objective medical evidence of injuries consistent with assault.
     - General plausibility that corruption exists in Vietnam and that some individuals might be exploited notwithstanding formal legal exemptions.

   On balance, an English court or tribunal would likely find that **Mr. Ho has not given a sufficiently credible account** of targeted, ongoing persecution on the specific basis claimed. The medical evidence supports that he was injured but does **not** firmly tie those injuries to the alleged persecutors or show a pattern of persecution.

4. **Risk on return, Convention reason, and state protection**

   Even if the court gave him some benefit of the doubt and assumed there had been at least one extortion‑linked assault, it would still need to assess future risk and legal sufficiency.

   a. **Future risk of serious harm**

   - There is no clear evidence of:
     - Recent threats;
     - Ongoing interest in him personally after a substantial passage of time; or
     - Any systematic tracking of him by those individuals.
   - His narrative suggests localised harm from a specific group, not a nationwide pattern of targeting him.
   - On this record, a tribunal may well find he has **not shown a real risk of renewed serious harm** now, years later, particularly if he could return to a different part of Vietnam.

   b. **Convention reason**

   - The alleged motivation of the persecutors appears to be **financial gain** (extortion/bribes) rather than his political opinion, religion, etc.
   - He has not suggested that he expressed anti‑government or anti‑military views, or that his father’s martyr status made him politically suspect. Instead, he says they exploited his exemption to extort money.
   - A nexus to a Refugee Convention ground is therefore weak:
     - Extortion for money, even by people abusing official position, typically does **not** amount to persecution “for reasons of” political opinion or other protected grounds, unless there is clear evidence that the targeting is linked to such a ground.
   - On the evidence, the tribunal is unlikely to find a sufficient Convention nexus, even if some harm is accepted.

   c. **State protection and internal relocation**

   - Vietnam is a functioning state with a national police apparatus. While corruption exists, there is no presented evidence (from country background material) that:
     - The state **systemically refuses** to act against such extortion; or
     - Victims of this kind of crime have no realistic recourse.
   - Without country material showing systemic state failure, *Horvath* and *Bagdanavicius* suggest the tribunal should generally find that **sufficient protection is available**.
   - Moreover, if the threat is localised to a particular area or group, internal relocation within Vietnam is a realistic option, *unless* there is evidence that those individuals have nationwide reach—which is absent here.
   - Thus, even on a partially accepted factual basis, Mr. Ho would likely fail to show that:
     - The Vietnamese authorities are unable or unwilling to protect him; and
     - He cannot safely relocate elsewhere in Vietnam.

5. **Effect of Section 8 (2004 Act)**

   - Section 8 obliges the court to treat his late claim, lack of initial disclosure of true injury causes, and making his claim only after a deportation notice as **adverse to credibility**.
   - The tribunal must still consider the whole evidence in the round, but here the adverse factors are substantial, and the supporting evidence is limited.
   - Applying s.8 correctly, the court is likely to conclude that the threshold of a “reasonable degree of likelihood” that his full story is true is **not met**.

6. **Conclusion**

   Putting matters together:

   - **Credibility**: seriously undermined by late claim, prior admitted dishonesty, lack of complaints, and absence of corroboration of the extortion story beyond his own word.
   - **Convention nexus**: insufficient; the harm described is best characterised as criminal extortion for financial motives.
   - **Future risk / Protection**: no convincing evidence of an ongoing, real risk across Vietnam, nor of systemic lack of state protection or impossibility of internal relocation.

   On the law and on the evidence as outlined, an English court is likely to find that Mr. Ho has **not discharged the (relatively low) burden of showing a real risk of persecution or Article 3 ill‑treatment on return**. His account does not meet the requirements of the Refugee Convention or of humanitarian protection when assessed under the Asylum and Immigration (Treatment of Claimants, etc.) Act 2004 and relevant case law.

- He must show this to a **“reasonable degree of likelihood”** (lower than the balance of probabilities, but still requiring a coherent, credible account).
- Under **s.8 AITCA 2004**, certain types of conduct (late claim, deception, etc.) must be taken **into account as damaging credibility**, but they are not automatically fatal.

I will go through the main issues: (1) credibility and s.8, (2) the medical evidence and alleged assaults, (3) the claimed military‑service/bribery basis, (4) Convention nexus and risk on return, and (5) overall assessment.

---

### 1. Credibility and Section 8 factors

**Late claim**

- Mr. Ho only claimed asylum **after deportation proceedings were initiated** following his criminal conviction.  
- Under **s.8(4)** this is conduct that a tribunal must treat as **damaging his credibility**, because it is, in general, suggestive of an attempt to avoid removal rather than the action of someone genuinely fleeing persecution.
- Case law (e.g. *JT (Cameroon) v SSHD* [2008] EWCA Civ 878) confirms that such factors are not determinative on their own; credibility must still be assessed “in the round”. But here, the timing does legitimately weigh against him.

**Dishonesty / inconsistent accounts**

- He accepts that he **gave false causes for his injuries** to medical personnel in Vietnam. His explanation is that he feared the perpetrators and therefore lied to avoid repercussions.
- Tribunals often accept that victims of violence may lie about sensitive matters in some contexts, but equally this shows he is **capable of giving untrue explanations** when he thinks it is self‑protective. This weakens his credibility generally and is clearly relevant under s.8.
- His **serious criminality** (cannabis production) is also conduct that can damage credibility in the tribunal’s eyes—though it doesn’t in itself answer the question whether he faces persecution, nor does it automatically bar refugee status unless it meets exclusion thresholds (which this offence, as described, almost certainly does not).

**Overall on s.8**

On a proper application of s.8 and the case law:

- The late claim and admitted dishonesty are significant **adverse credibility factors**, but not conclusive.
- They require the tribunal to **approach his account with caution**, and to look carefully for corroboration or objective support.

---

### 2. The medical evidence and what it proves

Mr. Ho has medical records from **two independent medical facilities** in Ho Chi Minh City (River Clinic and Maple District Hospital), documenting injuries arising from alleged assaults.  

These records support **two limited propositions**:

1. That he **sustained physical injuries** on at least one or more occasions.
2. That he attended recognised medical facilities in Vietnam and obtained treatment.

However, they do **not** directly evidence:

- **Who** attacked him;
- **Why** he was attacked (motive);
- That the perpetrators were state officials or persons acting in any quasi‑official capacity; or
- That the motive was extortion relating to alleged military‑service obligations.

The medical evidence is **neutral** on the central disputed points. It tends to corroborate that he **has been assaulted in the past**, but not the **narrative he attributes to those assaults**.

So:

- The medical evidence **supports him to the extent that he is not fabricating the fact of having been injured**.
- It does **not independently corroborate his claim** that corrupt actors linked to military service extorted him or that he is being persecuted in a way that raises a Convention‑based risk on return.

---

### 3. The military service / bribery narrative

This is the core of his case.

**Official documentation on exemption**

- There is official documentary evidence that Mr. Ho’s **father’s martyr status** is recognised and carries a **formal exemption from military service**.
- On its face, that undermines Mr. Ho’s central claim: he says he was targeted for bribes because of problems concerning military service exemption, but the **objective evidence says there was in fact no legal obligation for him to serve**.

He responds by saying:

- Official policy and exemption are one thing, but he was still victimised by **local corrupt officials or local power networks** who ignored or subverted that exemption.
- This is **not inherently impossible**: in many countries, corruption means local practice diverges from law. But it must still be supported by evidence consistent with the **particular story he tells**, not just a generic possibility.

**Lack of corroboration on bribes and extortion**

He provides:

- No **receipts or bank records** relating to bribe payments;
- No **witness statements** from family members, neighbours, or friends in Vietnam attesting to the extortion;
- No evidence of any **approach to any higher‑level authority** (e.g. provincial or central) to complain of being wrongly targeted despite possessing a martyr‑status exemption;
- No documentation about the **identity or institutional affiliation** of those allegedly extorting him.

In the asylum context, one cannot require perfect corroboration, especially where corruption is alleged, but:

- Where the claimant’s **central narrative is directly in conflict with official records**, and his overall credibility is already weakened by s.8 factors, tribunals are entitled to look for **some plausible corroboration** if it reasonably could exist.
- Here, the narrative is not just “I was assaulted by criminals”; it is “I was repeatedly targeted, over time, by individuals exploiting military‑service rules, despite an exemption”. With documented martyr‑status exemption, that is a **specific and inherently testable claim**.

Given that conflict between his account and the official evidence:

- The absence of **any** supporting evidence from Vietnam (beyond medical records consistent with generic violence but not its cause) weighs heavily against his version.

**Plausibility**

It is plausible in the abstract that:

- Local actors might exploit conscription or exemptions for profit.
- Victims might be reluctant to report such extortion to the same corrupt or complicit authorities.

But the tribunal’s focus is not whether a **scenario** is imaginable, but whether **this particular story is reasonably likely to be true**. Here:

- His own documentary record shows there was **no legal need for him to serve**.
- He offers no example of any concrete attempt to rely on the martyr exemption in resisting the demands (e.g. showing an exemption certificate and still being forced, or being told the papers were worthless), nor independent evidence that those specific corrupt actors exist or are connected to him personally.

On these facts, it is open and, indeed, likely for a tribunal to find that:

- While he may have suffered assaults, his account of the **motive (military‑service extortion) and the sustained campaign** is not shown to a reasonable degree of likelihood.

---

### 4. Nexus to a Convention ground and risk on return

Even if one assumes some extortion took place, two additional hurdles arise:

**(a) Nexus to a Convention reason**

Bribery/extortion by corrupt officials or criminals is often **criminal or opportunistic**, not persecution “for reasons of” political opinion, religion, etc.

Possible arguments for nexus:

- He is being persecuted for a **political opinion**: refusal to accede to corrupt demands might be framed as anti‑corruption political stance.
- He belongs to a **particular social group** (e.g. family of martyrs) targeted for extortion.

But:

- His own case is that he *should* have been exempt from military service because of his father’s martyr status, and that the extortion took advantage of an alleged obligation or problem with that status—he does not clearly present it as punishment for expressing political dissent.
- There is no country‑specific evidence presented that “children of martyrs” who resist extortion are persecuted as a group, as opposed to being potential **economic targets**.

Given this, a tribunal may well find that, even if some harassment occurred, it was **ordinary criminal extortion** lacking a Convention nexus.

**(b) Prospective risk and sufficiency of protection**

For refugee status, Mr. Ho must show that:

- There is a **real risk** of future serious harm (to the Refugee Convention or ECHR Article 3 threshold) if returned; and
- The Vietnamese state is **unwilling or unable to provide reasonable protection**, or that internal relocation is not a viable alternative.

Here:

- The evidence of ongoing targeting is thin—no recent threats, no indication that his alleged attackers have been looking for him since his departure.
- Vietnam is a large country. There is nothing specific in the facts suggesting he could not **internally relocate** to another area away from the individuals he claims targeted him, particularly given that the alleged dispute is personal and localised rather than national.
- There is no indication that he is known nationally as a political opponent or that central authorities see him as an enemy.

On this record, it would be difficult for him to establish that:

- The **same agents** still have both the desire and the reach to target him throughout Vietnam; or
- The **state as a whole** would deny him protection if approached, as opposed to there being generalised corruption problems in some locations.

---

### 5. Balancing everything “in the round”

When credibility is assessed holistically—as required by UK asylum law and by the proper approach to s.8—the tribunal should weigh:

**Factors in Mr. Ho’s favour:**

- Genuine **medical evidence** of injuries, consistent with him having suffered assaults in Vietnam.
- A potentially **plausible general narrative** that local corruption can override formal legal protections, including in relation to military service.
- Explanation that fear of corrupt authorities may deter people from going to the police or approaching official bodies.

**Factors against him:**

- **Section 8 factors**: late asylum claim only after being notified of deportation; admitted lies to medical personnel; serious criminal conduct in the UK.
- **Direct contradiction** between official documents (confirming legal exemption from military service) and his claim that the core problem arose from obligations concerning that service.
- **Lack of corroborating evidence** of the key elements of his story: no proof of bribes, no witness evidence from Vietnam, no demonstration that he sought any kind of higher‑level remedy or assistance, and no identification of his alleged persecutors in a way that can be checked.
- No clear, cogent **Convention nexus** (persecution flowing from political opinion, social group, etc.) rather than from opportunistic criminality.
- No strong evidence of a **current, ongoing risk** that would persist after a return, particularly given the realistic possibility of **internal relocation** within Vietnam.

On that balance, an English court or tribunal would be justified in concluding:

- Mr. Ho has probably been **a victim of violence** in the past, but
- He has **not shown, to the lower standard of reasonable likelihood**, that the violence arose from the specific, structured pattern of extortion related to his military‑service status as claimed; nor that it amounts to persecution for a Convention reason; nor that he faces a present, real risk of such persecution anywhere in Vietnam today.

Accordingly, he does **not satisfy the requirements for asylum**. Similar reasoning would likely lead to the rejection of a stand‑alone humanitarian protection claim, in the absence of evidence of a real Article 3 risk on return.

Given the facts as presented, the court should uphold the Secretary of State’s decision.

I’ll walk through the analysis in two parts:

1. Whether the “transfer” is treated as made before or after the cutoff date for relief under § 2055(e)(3), in light of the 1982 codicil.
2. Whether the breadth of Kevin Fletcher’s life interest and the 1988 judicial reformation satisfy § 2055(e)(3)'s requirements for a charitable deduction.

---

## 1. Timing of the “transfer” and effect of the 1982 codicil

### a. The statutory framework

Section 2055(e) was enacted in response to the 1969 split‑interest rules, which sharply limited estate tax charitable deductions where a charity’s remainder interest followed a noncharitable interest (like a life estate) unless the arrangement took one of a few “approved” forms (charitable remainder annuity trust, charitable remainder unitrust, pooled income fund, etc.).

Congress later added § 2055(e)(3) as a remedial provision to *save* certain pre‑existing testamentary structures that did not technically qualify, provided:

- The “transfer” to charity was made before a cutoff date; and  
- The instrument was timely “reformed” by court order into a qualifying form without increasing the noncharitable interest.

Thus, the Government’s threshold argument is that the relevant “transfer” was not made until 1982, when the last codicil was executed, which would move the trust outside the statutory grandfathering.

### b. When was the “transfer” “made”?

The relevant “transfer” here is the testamentary transfer created by Mary Winston’s will that split her property into:

- A life interest for Kevin Fletcher; and  
- A remainder interest for Elmwood University.

That transfer was created by the 1971 will. The later codicils did not:

- Revoke the will or its dispositive scheme,  
- Eliminate or substitute the charitable remainderman (Elmwood remained the remainderman), or  
- Change the fundamental nature of the split between a noncharitable life estate and a charitable remainder.

They only altered the *amount* and mechanics of Kevin’s benefits during his lifetime.

In federal transfer tax law, a codicil generally is treated as republishing the will as of the date of the codicil, but that doctrine is not applied woodenly to defeat grandfathering where:

- The basic dispositive scheme remains intact, and  
- The changes are incremental adjustments that do not create a *new* transfer, but merely modify an existing one.

Courts facing similar grandfathering questions (in the estate, gift, and GST tax contexts) regularly distinguish between:

- A codicil that makes a fundamentally new transfer (for example, first creating a charitable remainder or materially changing the class of takers), versus  
- A codicil that tweaks beneficial interests without changing the underlying structure or the existence of the charitable remainder.

Here, the latter is the case. The 1971 will already created a life interest and a charitable remainder. The 1972, 1977, and 1982 codicils refined the specifics of Kevin’s benefits but did not alter the existence of Elmwood’s remainder or the split‑interest structure.

Under that reasoning, the “transfer” for purposes of § 2055(e)(3) was “made” in 1971, and the testamentary plan qualifies as pre‑cutoff. The codicil did not restart the clock.

---

## 2. Uncertainty of the remainder and the effect of post‑mortem reformation

The Government’s second major contention is that—even if timing is satisfied—the original terms of Kevin Fletcher’s interest rendered Elmwood University’s remainder so unascertainable that no charitable deduction could ever be allowed, and that the 1988 reformation cannot cure this problem.

### a. Original form: broad, potentially open‑ended life interest

Under the 1971 will and codicils, Kevin Fletcher—already elderly at Mary’s death—was entitled to:

- Monthly payments;  
- Coverage of his medical expenses and taxes;  
- Upkeep and *improvements* of the Riverside residence; and  
- Other expenditures.

No explicit numeric limits or objective standards were set. That, standing alone, would normally be fatal to a charitable remainder deduction under the usual rule: the charitable remainder must be “presently ascertainable” and “severable from the noncharitable interests” as of the decedent’s death so that its value can be computed with reasonable certainty.

In particular, the open‑ended authority to spend principal on:

- Uncapped medical expenses at an advanced age, and  
- Unspecified “improvements” and “other expenditures”

makes it impossible, at the moment of death, to compute with precision how much will remain for Elmwood. That is precisely the problem Congress sought to avoid in the general § 2055 rules.

If the analysis stopped there, the Government’s position on ascertainability would be strong.

### b. But § 2055(e)(3) is *specifically designed* to address that defect

However, § 2055(e)(3) *exists to deal with this precise situation*: a pre‑cutoff split‑interest transfer that does not, as originally drafted, meet the form and actuarial ascertainability requirements, but that the estate is allowed to *fix* post‑mortem.

Key features of § 2055(e)(3):

1. It explicitly authorizes post‑death “reformation” of a testamentary instrument that created both a charitable and noncharitable interest so the charitable remainder will “qualify for a charitable deduction.”  
2. If the reformation occurs within the statutory time limits and does not increase the noncharitable beneficiary’s interest, the resulting qualification is treated as effective *as of the decedent’s date of death*. The reformation “relates back.”  
3. The approved reformed forms include arrangements (such as annuity interests) that, once fixed, are actuarially determinable under the Treasury Regulations.

Harper Bank, as trustee, did exactly what the statute contemplates:

- It went to state court in 1988 and obtained a judicial order reforming Kevin’s interest to a fixed annual amount—i.e., a classic annuity payout tied to the trust.  
- A fixed annuity payable for a life is the paradigmatic “ascertainable” interest that can be valued under standard mortality tables and used to determine the remainder value as of Mary Winston’s 1985 death.  
- There is no indication that the reformation increased Kevin Fletcher’s economic benefit; rather, it converted a potentially larger, open‑ended interest into a measured, fixed amount.

### c. The Government’s “date of death only” argument conflicts with § 2055(e)(3)

The Government argues that qualification must be tested solely “as of the date of death based on the terms then in effect,” rendering post‑mortem judicial fixes irrelevant.

That position is inconsistent with the very text and structure of § 2055(e)(3):

- The whole point of the provision is to permit nonconforming pre‑cutoff arrangements to be **retrofitted**—after death—into conforming structures.  
- The statute would be meaningless if the Government’s rule were accepted; no reformation would ever matter because the instrument would have already failed as of the date of death.  
- Congress deliberately relaxed the strict “as drafted at date of death” rule for this special class of pre‑cutoff transfers, explicitly so that estates could correct technical drafting deficiencies without sacrificing the decedent’s charitable intent.

The requirement that the reformation relates back to the date of death answers the Government’s policy concern: the deduction is allowed not because the IRS tolerates non‑qualifying forms at death, but because—after reformation—the law treats the qualifying form as if it had been in place at death.

As long as:

- The original arrangement was a qualifying split‑interest transfer made before the statutory cutoff,  
- The reformation was timely and court‑ordered,  
- The new form meets the statutory/regulatory requirements (here, an annuity interest plus a charitable remainder), and  
- The noncharitable interest was not increased,

then under § 2055(e)(3) the charitable remainder is deductible.

All of those conditions appear satisfied:

- The testamentary transfer was made in 1971.  
- The reformation into a fixed annuity interest occurred in 1988 pursuant to state court order—within the remedial timelines Congress allowed.  
- A fixed annuity in favor of a life beneficiary with the remainder to charity is explicitly recognized as an acceptable structure.  
- Nothing suggests Kevin’s interest was enlarged; if anything, it was narrowed and made more predictable.

### d. Statutory purpose supports allowing the deduction

Congress enacted § 2055(e)(3) to prevent forfeiture of charitable deductions in cases where:

- The decedent’s charitable intent is clear;  
- The charity’s remainder is genuine and not a sham; and  
- The technical failure lies in the drafting of the intervening noncharitable interest, not in any attempt to defeat the charitable policy of the statute.

Mary Winston’s plan fits squarely into that category:

- She consistently provided that, after Kevin Fletcher’s life interest, Elmwood University would receive the remainder.  
- The codicils never undermined that charitable remainder; they simply adjusted what Kevin could receive during life.  
- Harper Bank sought reformation not to game the system but to align the instrument with the forms the Code and regulations require.

Denying the deduction in this setting would undermine § 2055(e)(3)’s remedial objective and punish a testator for defects Congress specifically authorized courts and estates to cure.

---

## Conclusion

Because:

1. The relevant “transfer” was made in 1971 when the will first created the split‑interest arrangement, and the later codicils did not constitute a new post‑cutoff transfer; and  
2. The 1988 judicial reformation validly converted Kevin Fletcher’s broad life interest into a fixed annuity interest, making Elmwood University’s remainder actuarially ascertainable as of Mary Winston’s death, in the manner expressly sanctioned by § 2055(e)(3);

a U.S. court should hold that the estate is entitled to an estate tax charitable deduction for the remainder interest to Elmwood University.
